chapters.title: Scene 1 - Declaration 1
chapters.content:
When I was a little boy in Eunpunggol,

there was a high-school girl named Seonju
who lived near the village clinic.

On days when our house felt strangely quiet,
I would wander into their yard.

She would teach me things—
arithmetic, spelling,
simple lessons like that.



Her father, Dr. Cha,

often treated me because I was a sickly child.

Whenever I told them,
"I want to marry Seonju!"

the two of them would exchange a smile and say,

"You can marry when you become an adult."

So I asked,
"What's an adult?"

Dr. Cha chuckled.

"When you grow healthy
and can beat the elders in this village,
then you're an adult."

I nodded seriously.

"Then if I beat the elders,
I'll marry Seonju."

Dr. Cha laughed.

"Of course! Then you must marry her.
Seonju, you'll have to keep that promise too."

Seonju smiled and said,

"I'll wait for the day Dong-gi becomes an adult."


One autumn afternoon,
I was playing janggi with the elders.

I was the youngest at the board,
but nobody in Eunpunggol went easy on anyone.

Dr. Cha and Seonju sat across from me,
waiting for my move.

And for some reason—
maybe the sun,
maybe pride,
maybe just a child's heart bursting at the seams—

the words shot out of my mouth.

chapters.title: Scene 2 - Declaration 2
chapters.content:
"So, Doctor...
you wanna play this match with me?

For your daughter?"

The world stopped.

I tapped a piece, leaned in, and whispered:

"I can beat you in twenty moves."

Dr. Cha blinked at me—
a polite kid turned tiny warrior.

"Look at this little punk!" he shouted,
half furious, half amused.

The elders exploded.

Someone slapped his thigh.
Someone choked on his tobacco.
Someone muttered,

"This boy's either blessed or doomed."

But my fists stayed curled,
cheeks burning,
heart flying.

For the first time,
I wasn't a lonely kid.

I was a boy
who dared to say his dream aloud.

Then came the real negotiation.

Dr. Cha:
"You want something big?
What is it?"

Me:
"Seonju. Your daughter.
Play me with any handicap you like."

Dr. Cha:
"Negotiation?
What do I get if I win the game?"

Me:
"A cow for the village carnival.
Worth the price of a house.
Isn't that enough?"

Dr. Cha:
"OK. Deal.
No mercy. You know?"

Me:
"Call.
No retreat."

He squinted, realizing
this was the same boy
who once endured ten stitches
without a drop of anesthetic.

A boy like that
only bets big for one thing.

And the game began.

My reckless Nongpo attack.
Two po slicing through his cha in seven moves.
Trading my cha for his in ten moves.
A fortress rising around my king by the fifteenth.

By the twentieth move,
I whispered,

"Doctor... it's over."

He stared.

Then nodded.

"Good game, boy."


The elders roared
like we'd just won the World Series.

Then one old man asked,

"Hey kid!
What do you know about honeymoon night?"

I puffed my chest.

"I know!
It's really important."

"Then tell us."

So I did.

"My mom gives me a smelly soft chunk of doenjang.
I hide it and stick it
on my wife's butt while she's sleeping.

That way she won't look down on me
just because I'm little!"

Silence.

Then the world blew up.

Men falling sideways,
someone coughing his lungs out,
someone yelling for air.

Someone whispered,

"Kid...
you should've kept that secret.
Seonju probably heard everything."

I grinned.

"She'll pretend to be fooled.

That's why I chose her.

That's wisdom, not ignorance."

That finished them.

Even Dr. Cha couldn't hide his smile,
though he half-feared
I might faint from excitement.

Finally he yelled,

"Seonju!
Take this boy home
before he explodes!"

She knelt.

I climbed onto her back.

"Nuna...
I'm sleepy..."

My arms slid around her neck
as her footsteps thumped warm and steady.

And for one perfect moment,
I thought—

If this is what forever feels like...

I could stay here
a long, long time.

chapters.title: Scene 3 - Measle
chapters.content:
Seonju-nuna knew my house well,

so she carried me straight home on her back.

She laid me on my bed and turned as if to leave—

but something was wrong.

She felt it before she understood it.

On the way,

my body heat kept soaking through her shirt.

At first, she thought it was just excitement,

that warm sweat kids get after playing too hard.

But this was different—

too hot, too heavy, too steady.

She touched her own forehead,

then mine.

"...Fever."


She called my family first,

then her father, Dr. Cha.

He came quickly,

checked my pulse, my eyes, my tongue—

and finally said quietly,

with a weight only adults understand:

"It looks like measles."

Back then, in my hometown,

measles was called the little grim reaper—

the guide who took children

before they had a chance to grow.

Dr. Cha left to gather medicine.

But Seonju didn't leave.

Not even for a breath.

She stayed.

She helped me swallow the bitter medicine,

tilted my head just right,

wiped my mouth gently.

She changed the wet cloth on my forehead

again and again

until her own hands smelled faintly

of cool water and worry.

Outside,

my mother placed a bowl of clean water

on the stone platform by the jangdokdae

and prayed with trembling hands.

Seonju joined her—

two women,

two hearts,

praying like every breath

might drag me back from the river's edge.

A month passed like that—

slow, heavy, endless.

When I could finally sit up,

my mother looked at Seonju and sighed.

"Seonju...

go home now.

It's time."

But Seonju-nuna

shook her head so hard her braid swung.

"Mom...

I can't leave my little groom now.

Please...

let me stay near him."

My mother let out a long, tired breath—

part relief,

part surrender—

and muttered,

"You're too much...

truly too much..."

chapters.title: Scene 4 - A tale that wasn't a Lie
chapters.content:
When I was halfway recovered—

able to walk, able to eat—

Seonju-nuna still treated me like a hospital nurse

who refused to clock out.

One warm autumn afternoon,

I was sitting on a wooden flower-shaped stool under the sunlight.

Every single hour,

she touched my forehead with her soft, silk-like hand

to check my temperature.

It felt comforting.

Too comforting.

Comforting in a way our strict old village would never approve of

between an unmarried girl and a boy.

So I muttered, half-shy, half-serious:

Me: "Nuna... I'm almost recovered.

You don't have to do this much anymore."

Seonju: "Not yet.

You're not fully recovered."

Me: "Don't worry.

I already punished all the Jeoseung-saja (grim reapers)."

She burst into a tiny giggle,

eyes wide, amazed and curious.

Seonju: "Oh really?

And how did you beat them, huh?"

I straightened my back like a warrior telling an epic.

Me: "When the Jeoseung-saja came to take me,

I told them,

'I have a message from your boss.'

Your boss granted me a long, comfortable life in the real world

until his retirement.

Because I'm the official successor

to the Kingdom of Death."

Her eyes widened even more.

Seonju: "Successor?

Then what happened?"

So I continued my legend.

Me: "They didn't believe me,

so they dragged me to their king, Yeomra.

In front of him, I said:

'Your Highness!

Long time no see.

Your boys stupidly captured me again.'

And Yeomra said:

'Long time no see indeed—

no mail, no phone call.

You're my successor since you sacrificed yourself

saving your people 400 years ago

in the Joseon–Japan War...

as Admiral Yi Sun-sin.'"

Her jaw dropped.

I kept going, dead serious.

Me: "Yeomra said the last 400 years were rough.

Many grim reapers retired,

so new recruits didn't know who I was.

They only followed manuals and reports,

like amateurs.

So the King laughed—

a huge, royal laugh:

'You should come back and teach them right from wrong...

but first, take a 100-year vacation.

My boys made a big mistake.

What reward do you want?'

So I said:

'Your Highness,

let me live with my new family in the real world.

And your boys—

they must not bother me or my family.'

And the King replied:

'You are always right.

You have my word, sealed by the scar on your left chest.

When my boys see that scar,

they must bow before your dignity.'"

I paused.

Looked at her.

Me: "So I came back to you."

She wiped her tears,

smiling like sunlight breaking into water.

Seonju: "Then... we're safe?

No danger anymore?"

ME: "Absolutely.

One million percent.

No worries."

She hugged me tightly,

buried her face on my shoulder.

Seonju: "Thank you...

for coming back.

For being safe.

For peace."

chapters.title: Scene 5 - The Agreement
chapters.content:
My parents watched Seonju for weeks—

then months—

the way farmers watch the first sprout in spring

and quietly know this one will grow tall.

They didn't say it aloud,

but I felt it in the way Mother folded laundry near her,

and the way Father cleared his throat

whenever she poured him tea.

One evening, Father finally invited Dr. Cha for tea.

Our living room was small but proud—

a tea table polished smooth by years,

a long aisle from the kitchen,

and a Sony TV with a blinking VCR light

on the opposite wall, like a tiny lighthouse.

Father, with a cup of Ceylon laced with a fingertip of brandy,

sat in his largest chair—

the throne of our house.

Dr. Cha sat across from him,

posture straight, eyes calm,

a man who had pulled countless children from fever.

Mother placed coffee before the guest

and quietly sat beside Father.

The room settled

like dust after a long day's harvest.

Then Father spoke—

his voice low, warm,

but with the weight of decisions that change lives.

Father:

"Mr. Cha... your daughter—our Seonju—

she is precious to us.

Kind. Steady. Wise beyond her years.

My boy seems to hope

to walk the rest of his life with her."

Dr. Cha lowered his gaze,

thinking.

Dr. Cha:

"Your son...

smart, polite, brave,

and sometimes frighteningly determined.

Young, yes—

but easily the most grown of any child I've met."

Father nodded, satisfied.

Father:

"My belief is simple:

when someone has ability,

the world must not waste it.

He should receive what fits him."

Dr. Cha:

"Fate... is not equal to all.

Some children are born with paths

cut deeper and brighter than others.

Your son is one of them."

A long silence passed—

the kind men share

before agreeing on something bigger than themselves.

Then Father said, quietly but firmly:

Father:

"Let's join the two.

Let them marry.

Let them be blessed."

Dr. Cha breathed in—

slow, deep.

Dr. Cha:

"I agree with your heart...

but my daughter is still a student."

Father:

"She will finish school.

After that—

I'll send them both abroad.

Let them study.

Grow.

Build a life wider than this valley."

Dr. Cha laughed softly,

half disbelief, half relief.

Dr. Cha:

"That...

that is more than enough.

More than I hoped."

Father turned to Mother:

Father:

"Honey—

prepare the wedding clothes, the jewelry, the small things she'll need."

Dr. Cha protested with a smile.

Dr. Cha:

"What should I prepare, then?"

Mother:

"Just the things she already used.That is enough."

And it was.

chapters.title: Scene 6 - Sharpness unvailed
chapters.content:
That very week,

Father sent workers to remodel a small house on the edge of the field—

a house meant for the two of us,

where the riverbend wind always arrived first.

After that day,

my wedding with Seonju

became an unspoken, unstoppable truth

throughout Eunpunggol.

Even the wind seemed to know.

The house was half-remodeled,

wood dust floating in the warm afternoon breeze.

I sat on the floor, brushing my kitten's fur,

when my nephew—same age as Seonju—came wandering in.

He started teasing me, poking my shoulder,

asking nonsense questions.

I just answered, "Yeah? Uh-huh."

He looked bored.

Then he suddenly asked,

"Uncle...

did you ever touch her butt?

Or grab her breast?"

My hand froze.

In the next breath,

I grabbed him by the collar

and pulled the fruit knife from the table,

pressing it right under his jaw.


I roared:

"Say that again.

Say it!

You know who I am?

I'm the successor of this family!"

Workers rushed out, screaming.

No one dared get close.

My mother stood there, arms crossed—

not stopping me, not helping either—

just watching.

I shouted again:

"Butt? Breast?

You crossed the family law.

You understand what that means?"

No one answered.

Even the wind seemed to stop.

My nephew's mother burst into tears.

"Please—please forgive him!

He's stupid, thoughtless...

he doesn't know what he said!"

I lowered the knife just enough for him to breathe.

I said:

"Listen, boy.

I fight fire with fire for my family.

I bleed with my own blood for dignity.

That's our law.

That's our name."

My mother finally murmured,

"Enough.

He understands."

So I let him go.

Then I turned to everyone and spoke clearly, so the whole house heard:

"Listen well.

Looking down on my wife

is a challenge against me.

Anyone who crosses that line

will be thrown out of this village.

One rule.

One ruler.

Remember it."

I turned toward my room.

Seonju knelt down in front of me,

showing her back—her way of asking me to climb on.


But this time,

I walked on my own feet.

She followed quietly behind.

chapters.title: Scene 7 - Back from Death
chapters.content:
When I entered my room,

my knees gave out and I dropped to the floor like a rotten apple.

Seonju gasped.

She rushed to call my mother.

My mother came in,

took one long look at me,

and without raising her voice, summoned her people.

In less than an hour,

Mr. Ahn—normally a quiet farmer but our family's shadow in emergencies—

appeared, panting.

Mr. Ahn:

"Madam! What do you need?"

Mom:

"Go to Punggi. Find Dr. Kim.

Bring him.

Run."

Mr. Ahn:

"Yes, madam!"

He disappeared like smoke.

Mom chewed a tiny black herbal ball,

then pressed it into my mouth with her own lips,

dripping a little water after it.

She looked at Seonju as if saying,

Don't fear—but also, this is the moment to fear.

Two hours later,

Mr. Ahn returned with Dr. Kim.

Dr. Kim knelt beside me.

Dr. Kim:

"I heard the news...

It must have struck him like thunder.

Let me check him."

He checked my pulse,

lifted my eyelids,

studied my pupils.

Then he handed my mother a small bottle.

Dr. Kim:

"Madam...

this medicine needs blood."

Before he even finished the word blood,

Seonju bit her own finger.

A drop fell—

deep red—

onto the dark medicine.

She lifted my head into her arms

and fed me the mixture drop by drop,

her hands trembling.


When it was done,

she covered me with a blanket

and sat still, staring at me

as if her eyes alone could keep me alive.

For a long time,

nobody breathed.

Then—

my lips moved.

A small sound escaped.

Dr. Kim checked my pulse again.

Dr. Kim:

"...He's coming back.

Slowly.

He's crossing the line back from death."

Everyone exhaled at once.

Mother said quietly:

"No one speaks of today.

Not a word."

Mr. Ahn and Dr. Kim bowed and left.

Only then did Seonju break—

tears streaming down her face.

Seonju:

"Mom...

I thought I was protecting him.

But he...

he was protecting me."

My mother gently cleaned her wounded finger with cotton soaked in warm water.

Mom:

"I told my son to hide his sharpness.

A house like ours—where money flows—

always brings jealousy, schemes, and poison.

He learned to step lightly,

to speak carefully,

to survive quietly.

He grew up under threats you didn't see."

Mom took Seonju's trembling hand.

"But when he met you...

he felt safe for the first time.

So don't blame yourself.

From today on...

you stay beside him.

That's your place. Understand?"

Seonju nodded through tears.

"He is already my little groom.

I will never leave him alone."

chapters.title: Scene 8 - Lesser Guardians
chapters.content:
At that time outside—Dokkaebi & Messenger.

Dokkaebi was trotting along the barley field, sniffing the evening breeze like a dog who knew a few too many secrets, when he spotted a familiar gray figure hiding behind the persimmon tree.

The Grim Messenger was standing there—scythe polished, robe wrinkled, looking like a lost tourist from the afterlife.

Dokkaebi:
"Hey! What the heck are you doing here at this hour? It ain't midnight, and nobody's scheduled to die."

The Messenger nearly dropped his scythe.

Messenger:
"I—I'm here on official duty! Protecting Admiral Yi!"

Dokkaebi rolled his eyes so dramatically the barley stalks bowed with him.

Dokkaebi:
"Oh lord... You really don't see it, do you? Look at that house. Can't you see the glow?"

Messenger blinked once, twice, then finally noticed the soft red light shimmering around the house like a warm heartbeat.

Messenger:
"That... is that fire...?"

SMACK.

Dokkaebi slapped the back of his head.

Dokkaebi:
"Fire is what's burning inside your skull! That's a Pure Blood Shield, you idiot! A protection seal!"

Messenger:
"...Oh."

Dokkaebi:
"Not even ghosts can pass through that. Not senior messengers, not junior messengers, not you, not me."

Messenger looked horrified.

Messenger:
"Then... why did they send me here?"

Dokkaebi:
"To keep you OUTSIDE. Think of it as... afterlife patrol duty."

Messenger deflated like wet laundry and plopped onto the dirt.

Messenger:
"So... what do we do? Just... sit?"

Dokkaebi:
"Yap."

Messenger:
"And... wait?"

Dokkaebi:
"Correct."

Messenger:
"Until... when?"

Dokkaebi stared at the glowing house, the shield pulsing gently, wind brushing over the barley like a lullaby.

Dokkaebi:
"Until the Little Groom wakes up. After that, the King of Death will give us the next move."

Messenger nodded, trying to look wise but failing miserably.

Messenger:
"...So there was a grand plan."

Dokkaebi:
"Grand plan my ass. They just don't want you messing anything up."

Messenger shut his mouth.

They sat there quietly, the cicadas singing again, the shield warm and red like a living heartbeat.

After a long silence, the Messenger whispered:

Messenger:
"Hey... Dokkaebi... do you know why the shield's so strong?"

Dokkaebi snorted.

Dokkaebi:
"Because in that house sleeps the Little Groom... and the girl who spilled her own blood for him. That kind of bond? Even gods step back."

Messenger froze.

Messenger:
"...Her...? Her?"

Dokkaebi nodded like an ancient sage.

Dokkaebi:
"Yeah. Her. She bled for that boy tonight."

Messenger straightened up immediately, posture snapping into military discipline.

Messenger:
"Ah... yes... yes, that explains it. A blood vow. A full protection seal. I... I understand now."

Dokkaebi smirked.

Dokkaebi:
"You're learning. Finally."

The night settled around them.

The shield flickered softly.

Inside, a boy slept under blankets, and a girl kept watch beside him.

Outside, two ridiculous guardians of the underworld sat like scolded puppies—a dog scratching his ear with his foot, a messenger adjusting his oversized robe—both waiting for their tiny general to rise again.

chapters.title: Scene 9 - Peaceful Night
chapters.content:
When the remodeling was finally done,

my house—our house—

smelled of new wood and river wind.

The wedding followed.

Quiet.

Still.

Not because people weren't happy—

but because everyone

felt the weight of peace

settling over the village

like early snow.

That night,

I told my wife to prepare a feast—

the kind you make when a storm has passed

and the air tastes clean again.

I carried the food outside,

under the moon,

where the barley whispered

and the shield still pulsed faintly.

I cleared my throat,

looked toward the shadows under the persimmon tree.

Me:

"Hey—

you two idiots.

Don't pretend you're not there."

Dokkaebi's ears twitched.

The Messenger sat up straight

like a rookie soldier caught napping.

Me:

"Don't behave like children!

A few hundred years didn't make you adults?

Here—

my wedding gift."

I set down the food.

A whole tray—

steamed dumplings, honey rice cakes,

and a bowl of warm broth.

Me:

"Eat.

And behave.

No haunting.

No whispering.

No freaking out the neighbors.

Okay?"

Dokkaebi wagged his foot like a dog tail.

Messenger bowed like he was saluting a king.

Messenger:

"Congratulations, Admiral."

Dokkaebi:

"Yeah, yeah.

Long live the little groom."

I smirked.

The shield flickered once—

just enough for them to feel the warmth.

Me:

"And tell the King of Death—

I'll visit after harvest.

I'm busy right now."

Dokkaebi almost choked on a dumpling.

Messenger whispered, horrified:

"He... he can say things like that?"

Dokkaebi shrugged.

"That's our general.

Get used to it."

The night curled softly around us.

Inside the house,

my wife waited,

lamplight trembling gently like her breath.


Outside,

the two guardians ate my feast

like exiled puppies,

happy, confused,

but loyal—

waiting for the next impossible thing
I'd somehow make them do..

And that night,

for the first time since the fever,

the whole village slept

without fear.

chapters.title: Scene 10 - Doenjang Promise
chapters.content:
The morning after the wedding, Seonju was already out in the yard washing blankets.
Everyone in the village had heard about the "Doenjang Promise,"
so neighbors passing by chuckled and asked,

"So did you really make 'Doenjang' for the newlyweds?"

Mother called out from inside the house.

"Seonju! Leave that to the helpers.
Hey, Chungju! Where'd you go?"

Madam Chungju appeared from the doorway and answered,

"I was boiling the herbs, ma'am."

Then she walked over to Seonju,
held both of her hands warmly, and said with delight,

"Ah, Seonju!, it's so good to finally meet you properly in this house."

Mother continued,

"Chungju, make sure you teach Seonju everything—
which medicinal herbs Dong-gi must take,
which food he absolutely cannot eat.

And Seonju, you stick close to Madam Chungju
and learn how this household runs.

I'm not planning to make you a kitchen maid,
but you need to know how things work
if you're going to manage people."

Then she added,

"And starting next month,
you'll attend school in the town."

And so, Seonju followed Madam Chungju
from the herb storeroom to the kitchens,
learning every corner of the household step by step.

And I...0
I was finally allowed to become a child again.

But I knew there would be many eyes on her—
watching her, teasing her,
doubting her,
challenging her authority
within my family and across the whole village.

My mother would be the first among them.

But with my name behind her,
and with my place in this household,
she would be safer—
as long as she understood the weight of that name.


To be continued in Season 2...

chapters.title: Scene 1 - Riverside Wash Place (Summer)
chapters.content:
My village was wrapped in a long ripple of mountains,
full of granite and banded gneiss—
stones that drank every raindrop
and hid the water deep in their cold hearts.

In summer,
those stones gave us everything:
water to drink,
water to wash,
water to farm.

Water gathers,
becomes a pond,
spills into a river—
and that river chooses
where people will live.

One day,
my mother walked down to that riverside.
She polished the stones,
set each rock in its place,
and made what would become
the Enpung riverside wash place.

When the summer sunset melted over the valley,
the village women came down—
laundry on their backs,
children in their arms.

After washing the clothes,
every mother washed her child too.

"Blow your nose—
Heung~!"
Then she rinsed the little nose clean
under the running water.

The Night of the Flashlight

One summer night,
my mother headed to the wash place
with my wife.

"Seonju!
Let's go wash the laundry.
Bring the soap and towels!"

Before leaving,
she stopped by the warehouse—
probably to grab something
she'd hidden for exactly this moment.

While she was gone,
I leaned close to my wife
and whispered:

"You must enter the water after my mom
and come out before my mom."

She blinked.
"What for?"

"Just keep my word.
No questions."

Then my mother returned—
holding an old military flashlight,
the metal-cap kind
that looked like it had survived a war.

When we reached the riverside,
she clicked the light on
and swept every corner
like she was hunting ghosts.

One by one she shouted,
calling out the mothers:

"Who's there?
Byeong-ha's mom!"

Another sweep.

"And who's here this time?
Gyuhag's mom!"

Then the beam caught someone
and she gasped dramatically:

"Wait... who is that?
My my my...
look at that silky skin—
Chungju!!"

The entire river exploded.

The women shrieked,
scattering like chickens under a hawk.

"Oh my goodness!
Hyeongniiiiim~~~~!!"

Hands flying,
skirts swirling,
faces half laughing, half terrified.

But my mother wasn't finished.
She snapped the light again,
clicked her tongue,
and shouted:

"Chungju!
You deserve another marriage!
One more man!"

The riverside collapsed into a flood of laughter—
echoing, splashing, rolling along the valley.

She finally set the flashlight on a flat stone,
undressed with my wife,
and walked into the warm water.

My wife dressed first afterward—
faster than my mom,
faster than lightning.

My mother dressed next
and turned calmly...

But from the dark water
voices burst out:

"Where's my bra?"
"Where are my pants?"
"Where's my under—!!"

My mother cupped her hands
and shouted back:

"What are you looking for?
This white bra—
I saw you breastfeeding in it!
This beige one—
I saw G's whole backyard!
And this red one—"

The valley exploded again.

"Hyeongnim!!!
Seonju!!
Please stop your mother-in-law!!!"

But she was unstoppable.

"I can't return this red one!
Chungju!
The moment I show this to the men,
you'll find yourself a new husband!"

Women splashed and scattered—
laughing, screaming,
running in every direction
like sparrows startled by thunder.

One by one,

they grabbed whatever clothes they could,

half-dressed, half-laughing,

wrapping themselves in towels, skirts, aprons—

whatever their hands touched first.

Their laughter was a mess,

their footsteps were chaos,

and they vanished into the night

still cracking up under the summer sky.

For a moment,

the courtyard held its breath.

The last echo of their laughter drifted over the wall,

and the night quietly swallowed the commotion.

The lantern by the door swayed once,

softly—

as if even it was embarrassed to have witnessed all that.

I exhaled,

slow and warm,

like a man finally stepping out of a storm

into a quiet room.


After the Storm

When my wife returned to me,

her face was bright—

like someone who'd just danced with the summer moon.

I teased her softly:

Me:

"You looked like you had fun with Mom."

Seonju:

"Absolutely! I couldn't believe half of it!"

Me:

"What if my mom hid your clothes?"

Seonju (without a blink):

"I'd run straight to you, my little groom—

even if I had nothing on."

ME:

"That would be a spectacle.

The whole village would talk for a year."

Seonju:

"Yes.

A spectacle—

because I'm yours."

I shook my head, laughing quietly.

"You're terrible.

Really terrible..."

(But inside,

I hoped she would learn the order, the dignity,

the quiet bravery

my mother carried in her bones.)

Then I lay down and murmured:

"I'm sleepy.

Light the anti-mosquito incense.

I waited for you to come back safely...

and I want a peaceful night with you—

without those tiny little insects

ruining our first summer together."

She smiled,

soft and warm,

as if the whole night rested between us.

chapters.title: Scene 2 - The Smell of Ramyeon
chapters.content:
That night,

my mom was making Ramyeon.

I called The Messenger and Dokkaebi.
They came at once.

"Gentlemen," I asked,
"do you know this smell?"

The Duo:
"Yes sir!"

Me: "Answer in three seconds. Am I clear?"

The Duo (without hesitation):
"Yes sir!"

Me: "My mom's cooking is Michelin three-star level. Isn't it? Three~"

The Duo (immediate):
"Yes sir!"

Me: "Impressive. Tonight— there was absolutely no peeping-tom.Three~"

The Duo: "Yes sir!"

Me: "Very impressive. And you checked from start to end? Three~"

The Duo (proudly): "Absolutely, sir!"

Me: "Good. And you saw everything from start to end? Three~"

The Duo (with a smug little smile):"Of course, sir."

Me: "You saw everything from start to end??? Three... two—"

The Duo (instantly): "Yes, sir!!"

Me: "You sons of— Dinner's gone. Starve to death tonight."

The Duo: "???? !!!! ..."

I turned around and walked back inside.

I sighed and shut the door behind me.

"They saw nothing.
They learned nothing.
Hopeless idiots."

But as the door clicked shut,

I looked toward the dim houses of the village and thought:

"...The real men don't peek.
They just carry the world quietly on their backs."

And the smell of ramyeon curled around me—
soft, warm, and familiar—
like an arm I'd known all my life.


Afterwords, My mom appeared.

Mom: "On duty, you saw everything! Three, two—"
Duo: "Yes! We followed the duty!!!"

Mom: "Which bra color is the best?"
Duo: "Red one!!!!!"

Mom: gasping
"Children! You must learn much more!
Just eat the ramyeon before it gets cold."

chapters.title: Scene 3 - Riverside Wash Place (Winter)
chapters.content:
The cold of that era was merciless.

Winds swept down from the Arctic, Russia, Mongolia,

and the high mountains surrounding our village—

dry, cheek-cutting winds that felt sharp enough

to slice a breath in half.

People said that even people from Moscow

couldn't stand such wind and would retreat to their own lands.

It wasn't a joke.

That wind was truly that cruel.

But the mountain of laundry waiting for the village ladies

didn't care about weather.

It simply sat there—heavy as fate.

When the cold tightened its grip,

my mother called out to Byeongha's father.

"Byeongha's Fa!

Can you get the men to break the ice at the wash place?

Bring axes, hammers—whatever it takes, you know?"

And then he shouted across the village,

his voice rolling through the frozen air,

"Hey, boys!

The lady says we've got ice to break.

Grab your tools and get to the wash place—right now!"

Then the men gathered at the wash place,

carrying whatever they had—

even sickles, anything sharp or heavy enough.

They smashed the ice,

lifting the broken pieces onto the ground

with hammers, axes,

and sometimes even with their bare hands

when tools slipped on the frozen surface.

The women arrived soon after,

each carrying a mountain of laundry

in a hand-woven basket on one arm,

and a young child clinging to the other.

They settled into their familiar spots,

as if winter itself could not stop their day.

The men lit a fire

with dried wood and fallen branches

inside a big empty oil drum.

The flames rose fast,

and the smoke curled upward,

disappearing into the pale winter sky.

Cold made the ladies' hands freeze,

numb and almost without life.

They came up from the riverbank,

stretching their stiff fingers toward the fire,

trying to pull warmth back into their bones.


While they warmed their hands,

the men kept lifting fresh slabs of ice

and throwing them onto the ground

as if fighting a stubborn enemy.

When that day-long battle

between cold and laundry finally eased,

I walked down to the wash place

with two or three bunches of yangmiri—

dried smelt fish—

my small offering to the warriors of winter.

I threw the yangmiri, tied with a rope of twisted rice straw, straight into the fire.

The fish began to sizzle, its dried oil bubbling and darkening the flames.

I bit off a small piece to taste

—just to see if it was cooked enough—

then pulled the well-done yangmiri out one by one,

the rice straw already gone in the flames,

and laid them on a sheet of newspaper spread on the ground.

"Come on! Eat while it's hot!"

I shouted to everyone.

While the ladies and children ate the fish,

biting the warm flesh carefully,

the men watched them with quiet smiles.

When the washing was finally done,

the women lifted their hand-woven baskets—

filled with clean but still-wet clothes—onto their heads

and began the walk back home.

In each home,

there was a rope strung in the corner of the room,

beside the tiled floor laid over the heated stone— the fire-warmed ondol.

She or he lifted the wet laundry onto that rope.

The hot, dry air rising from the floor pulled the shimmering moisture out of the cloth before any bits of ice left on them could melt.

Soon the clothes dried stiff, hard and crinkled like thin wooden bark.

Men had to wait until the fire died down completely. If they poured water on it too soon, a burst of scalding steam would shoot up, burning them in an instant—

sometimes even taking a man's life, sometimes burning the very organs that carried his bloodline.

And worse, a single spark left alive could set the rice-straw roofs on fire.

If that happened, the whole village could fall in one night.

However, I climbed onto a big sheet of cracked ice,

and stood there holding a farmer's shovel like a captain.

The other children ran home, put on their black farm-work boots, and rushed back to the river to ride my one

When one child started to row, the others followed

But then one boy slipped and fell into the water.

He started crying right away—because crying was the best shield to protect him from his parents' scolding later.

At that moment, the men there sighed, "Again...?"

They lifted the boy out of the icy water and laid him on the ground.

The child sprang up and ran home, shouting "Mom!" as he cried.

And me—

shamefully, I fell into the water too.

Byeongha's Fa scooped me up, carried me on his back, and took me home.

I knew

"Again...?" was not out of annoyance,

but because they had grown up the same way—

falling into the water, being pulled out,

and learning winter by surviving it.

That's why they reached out to save us.

They knew exactly how it felt.

Arriving home,

my mom and my wife both gasped,

"What a troublemaker!"

then hurried to dress me in dry clothes.

My wife, puzzled by Mom's lack of scolding, asked quietly,

"Why didn't you warn him?"

My mom answered,

"Timing is everything.

He knows when it's his time to play."

I stepped out to the front gate of our house

and watched the last of the fire die out,

the men fading away into the winter dusk.

chapters.title: Scene 4 - Burned by Fire
chapters.content:
That night,

My kitten kept crying— not a normal "meow,"

but that ghost-detecting, tail-puffed,

I-saw-something-I-shouldn't-have kind of cry.

So I went outside.

And BAM—

the Messenger popped out of the dark

like someone who practiced jump-scares for a living.

Messenger: "Good evening, sir!"

Me: "Good evening?

You again?!

It's bedtime, man! Bedtime!"

Messenger: "Yes, sir... but I need help."

Me: "Help?!

I'm not customer service!"

Messenger: "It's... medicine.

For fire damage."

Me: "Fire damage??

Aren't you spirit people supposed to be immune to everything?

Holy, shiny, invincible—something like that?"

Messenger: "Dokkaebi is... different, sir."

Me: (arms crossed)

"Different HOW?"

Messenger: "He tried to kill the fire by...

peeing on it, sir."

Me: "OH. MY. GOD.

Tell him that is NOT a battle strategy!"

(Run into home)

A moment later I came out holding ointment like a doctor in a sitcom.

Me: "Here!

Rub this on his PRECIOUS part.

And for heaven's sake—

And don't let the female ghosts hear.

He'll NEVER live it down.

He's been single for centuries already."

Messenger: "Yes, sir! But..."

Me: "OH COME ON!

A BUT?! AGAIN?!

WHAT—WHAT—WHAT IS IT NOW?!"

Messenger: "Yangmiri.

One bunch.

Little one.

Pocket size.

PLEASE, sir..."

Me (gasping, staring up at the sky)

"My King...

You eternal child...

Fine.

Take it—and GO before the dawn shifts!"

chapters.title: Scene 5 - Garden of Pine Trees
chapters.content:
In my village, there was a play yard called the Garden of Pine Trees, Songjeong.

It was round in shape.
The west and south sides were lined with the small homes of our neighbors,
and the rest was guarded by tall pine trees
and old black stones that had stood there longer than memory.

In the far northern corner stood a nameless tomb—
a quiet mound everyone recognized,
but no one dared to claim.
Beside it lay a great flat stone.
We did not know it then,
but it was an ancient dolmen,
a relic from people who had lived and vanished centuries before us.

One autumn afternoon,
the children of the village—my friends and I—gathered at Songjeong.
We played catch,
our own rough version of baseball,
with a few worn gloves and a single tennis ball.

Back then, the country was changing fast.
Even we could feel the old military atmosphere fading.
The Seoul Olympics were on the horizon,
and in every elementary classroom,
there was at least one biography of Babe Ruth
sitting proudly on the must-read shelf—
as if his home runs could teach us how to dream bigger.

But none of that mattered to us that day.

We did not know who rested beneath that mound.
No name, no markers, no family left to visit.
So while we ran under the pines,
kicking dust, shouting, chasing each other through the sunlight,
a small thought kept passing through our hearts:

We're sorry, sir...
There's no one left to sit with you.
But if watching us play gives you even a moment of warmth,
please... stay with us.

Maybe that was why the autumn wind felt softer there,
why the shade of the dolmen never frightened us.
We believed—quietly, naturally—
that the one resting beneath the earth
looked over us with the gentle smile
of a grandfather who had no children left,
so he chose us instead,
like a grandfather we had never met.

We—Byeong-ha, Gyu-hak, Si-rak, Tae-hi, Sang-de, and I—
were just tossing and catching balls under the autumn sun.
Then the younger kids spotted us,
and one by one, like beads on a string,
they joined our circle.

We handed our baseball gloves to them,
letting the little ones feel like real players,
and sprinted home to grab anything we could use instead.

Some came back with worn-out workers' gloves.
One brought his father's leather mittens.
And I—
I marched in proudly holding a laundry bat,
lifting it like a hero brandishing his sword.

"There isn't a single ball in this whole village," I declared,
"that can escape this bat!"

For fun and practice,
I swung my proud laundry bat,
and the ball soared into the sky
like it wanted to see the whole village before coming down.

Then Si-rak—
the strongest,
the undefeated,
the legend of Songjeong—
stepped up,
spat on his hands,
and tightened his stance.

He smacked the ball so hard
it drew a perfect straight line across the afternoon air
and—CRACK!—
shattered someone's window on the far side of the garden.

Silence.
A heartbeat.
Then children exploded into screams and laughter,
scattering like sparrows chased by the wind.

Our positions formed instantly—
not through discussion,
not through fairness,
but by the mysterious instinct of children,
who somehow always know where to stand.


Only the pitcher and catcher stayed fixed.
Everyone else spread across the Garden of Pine Trees:
under the shade of the old pine roots,
beside the black stones,
near the nameless grave,
and even close to the dolmen,
which had been watching children play
for longer than any adult in the village could remember.

The younger brothers and sisters got to be hitters,
because we always threw the ball slowly for them—
big, generous, floating pitches.
And the umpire—basically whoever shouted loudest—
called every close pitch a walk,
so the little ones could run to first base proudly.

But when it was our turn,
the real game began.

We swung with every bone in our bodies,
chased balls like hungry tigers,
dived across the grass,
slid on the dirt,
and half the time ended up with bloody noses
and grass stuck to our foreheads.

Hyeon-suk nuna's catch was legendary.
She would grab her skirt with both hands,
run like the wind,
and scoop the ball just before it touched the ground.
Every time she did,
the whole field burst into laughter.


And if one of the little ones started crying,

I would kneel down,
tap the dust off their cheek,
pull out a candy ball from my pocket,
and say:

"Hey—crying kids don't get to play.
Only brave ones play here."

Instant magic.
Tears stopped.
The candy disappeared.
And peace returned to the Garden of Pine Trees.

Kids always needed to find their own older brothers or sisters.
They were all under our protection—
little shadows we had to keep within the circle.

Sometimes one of us had to leave early,
holding the hand of a younger sibling
and walking them to their parents' workplace.
We learned early that playtime itself
was the reward for helping our parents' world keep moving.

And when the sun dipped behind the hills,
the sound of our mothers calling our names
pulled us home one by one.

When I got back home,
my mom brushed the withered grass off me,
muttering under her breath,

"Troublemaker... again!!!"

Then she dragged me to the washbasin,
scrubbed the day's dust from my skin,
and dressed me in a clean set of clothes—
still shaking her head,
but with the corners of her mouth already soft with relief.

When I stepped into my room,
my wife was sitting there, watching TV.

Me: Honey! What are you doing?

Wife: No reaction. No answer.

Me: Honey? What are you watching?

Wife: Still nothing. Not a blink.

Me: What are you doing right now...?

Wife: (suddenly straightening up)
I can catch a flying ball like Hyeon-suk!!!

I sighed—softly, almost laughing.

Me:
Do you really want to be the nanny for every kid out there?
Kids always cling to the prettiest girl.
You don't know that?

Her voice softened immediately.

Wife:
Really?
But I feel like children here love playing at the Garden of Pine Trees
much more than those autumn school sports events...

I leaned closer, my voice gentle.

Me:
Autumn sports events are strange.
Kids spend more than a month practicing like soldiers,
and government officers come to supervise the whole thing.
How is that a children's festival?

Wife: (blinking, confused)
Strange... yeah.
Now that you say it, it really is strange.

That night,
my wife and I went back to the playing field.
I lifted my hand and shouted:

Me:
Back up!
A little farther—yeah, right there!
Get ready!


I tossed the tennis ball slow and high,
sending it climbing toward the night sky.

She started running.

Running—
sliding—
slipping—
catching—
falling—
bleeding.

I rushed over,
took her hand,
pulled her close,
and placed a candy ball in her palm.

Me:

Listen, kid...
crying girls don't get to join the baseball game.

chapters.title: Scene 6 - Compaints of Ghosts
chapters.content:
A few days later, the Duo came running to me.

Me: "Long time no see. Hey—fire boy.
How's your precious department doing, hmm?"

Dokkaebi: "Thanks to you, sir!! Much better now!!"

Me: "Good.
Girls don't like a bald head... or a bald other one, you know?"

I leaned in slowly—on purpose.

"And you? What is it today?
Lotus? Snickers? Rice cake? Spit it out."

Messenger (panicking): "N-no, sir!! Not food!!"

Then he giggled.
That cursed giggle that always means disaster.

Messenger: "Sir... we bring a notice."

Me: "...A notice? What notice."

Messenger: "A complaint, sir!!
The ghost community demands quiet hours in the Garden!!"

Me: "Ghost community, hmm."

I sighed like an emperor bored with politics.

"Fine. Go tell them this:
If they keep nagging...
I'll reveal their BIGGEST secret.
Especially that water ghost.
Her mouth moves faster than light, you know?"

Dokkaebi (shrinking instantly): "NO, sir! Please don't!!
I—I'll tell them about your generosity!!"

Me: "Good boy.
Now get out. Bye~"

As they ran away tripping over each other,
I turned around and nearly died laughing.

Because their schemes—
those tiny, pathetic, adorable little schemes—
are never hidden from me.

chapters.title: Scene 7 - The Rise of Legend
chapters.content:
When we were playing in the Garden,

there was always that one kid crying for absolutely no reason.

My friends tried everything to calm him.
But when their patience ran dry, they finally shouted:

"Hey! Boss! You take care of him!"

So I marched over, slapping my hand with my laundry bat like an angry schoolteacher about to hand out justice.


I stood solemnly in front of the crying kid."Who stopped our game?

And why are you crying, boy?"

He sniffled, scared.

"M-my... big brother...
He didn't play with me..."

Now here's the important part.

His real big brother—who also happened to be my closest friend—was standing right there watching.

In our village, your friend's younger sibling was practically your sibling.
If the younger one cried, his big brother would get scolded at home.

So comforting the younger kid was basically a rescue mission.

So I nodded slowly. Dramatically.

"I see.
Your big brother was a bad boy.
I will punish him IMMEDIATELY."

Then I grabbed my friend—yes, the real older brother—and gave him a fake spanking loud enough for the crying kid to hear.

"Ahya! Ugg! Hu!!"

(My friend overacted like a pro.)

The kids gathered around and shouted to the crying boy:

"Look! The Boss is MAD at your brother!
Your brother looks terrified! What should we do?!"

The boy instantly stopped crying and ran to me.

"Boss! Please forgive my brother!
I don't hate him... I just want to be with him..."

I crossed my arms like a judge.

"Your brother is unforgivable...
BUT—since you forgave him, he is free."

Then I pulled out my treasure—

a freshly braided strawberry-flavored candy ball—

and handed it to him.

He gasped.

"Thank you!
But... why do only you have these candies?"

I shrugged proudly.

"Because I'm rich.
And sympathetic."

"But... why are you rich?"

I sighed.
Curiosity truly has no end.

"Listen carefully.
Everyone here calls me 'General,' right?
It's a top secret, but I'll tell you."

The kids leaned in.

"I was Admiral Yi Sun-sin."

All jaws dropped.

I continued:

"When I was fighting Japanese soldiers,
I got shot and died.

I went to the Kingdom of Death.

King Yeomra judged me and said:

'Admiral Yi, you saved many people.
You deserve a 100-year vacation in the real world.
Be reborn as a rich man and rest.'

So when I returned,
I needed a body.

I chose this one."

The boy squinted.

"How can I believe you?"

I opened my shirt and showed him the old scar on my chest—

(the one from my childhood accident, but they didn't need to know that).

"Look.
A bullet scar from five hundred years ago.
Proof number one.

And my birthday?
Same as Admiral Yi Sun-sin's."

My friends all shouted in perfect harmony:

"It's TRUE!
That's why we call him Boss!
Even your parents know it!"The boy stared in awe.

"Then... can you take me on the Turtle Ship?"

I nodded seriously.

"I hid it near Hansan Island for emergencies.
I'm gathering brave and loyal people.

But YOU...

are a crying troublemaker.
I cannot take you."

The boy panicked.

"General!
I'll be a good boy!
I PROMISE!"

I touched his shoulder.

"Good boy.
Then someday... you can board the ship."

He brightened.

We returned to the baseball game.

And that was the day the whole village started calling me "General."

Because the hardest fight in the world
is not against an army—

but against a crying kid.

chapters.title: Scene 8 - Baseball Kit
chapters.content:
A few days later, I summoned the Duo.

"Gentlemen. This—"

I lifted a box.

"—is my gift for the ghost community.
They seem bored. Let them have fun."

The Messenger blinked.

"Base... ball kit, sir?"

"Yes. My village friends wanted to share it.
Isn't it touching?"

The Messenger's voice trembled.

"T-thank you, sir...! Really...!"

Dokkaebi peeked into the box, his tail almost wagging.

"Uh... sir... is that candy?
C-can I have the strawberry one...?"

"Yes, yes. Help yourself.
They're inside the—"

Dokkaebi froze.

"...Sir... There's no strawberry flavor."

Silence.

I slowly turned my head.

"You... son of... again?!

Get. Out. Of. My. Sight."

Dokkaebi fled so fast the ground shook.

The Messenger bowed ninety degrees and hurried after him.

I closed the door with a sigh.

"Ghosts these days...
No discipline. No wisdom.
And always—ALWAYS—after my strawberry candy."

chapters.title: Scene 9 - Little Genesis
chapters.content:
There was an old zelkova tree at the corner of the schoolyard.

Kids used to climb it, nap under it,
and sometimes read books in its shade.

But one day, something happened there—
something small, something quick,
but enough to make every adult in the village fall silent for a moment.

One kid slipped and fell straight from the tree.

Another froze for a heartbeat, then burst into tears.

One more went pale as a ghost, too scared even to breathe.

No blood. No broken bones.

But that wasn't the point.

It was the moment itself—
that split second when the grown-ups felt their chests tighten
and a cold wave run down their backs.

"...We were one step away from disaster."

The tree climbing they had brushed off as harmless play—
that single scare made them realize
how close it had always been to danger,
and how easily things could have gone terribly wrong.

A few days later, back in the village,
I was playing janggi with the uncles as usual

when I overheard them talking quietly—too quietly—
about that accident near the zelkova tree.

One uncle sighed.

Another shook his head.

And then, as if they had agreed beforehand,
they started speaking just loud enough
for the nearby children to hear.

"You know that zelkova tree behind the school, right?"
one uncle began.

"Under that tree... a Yimugi used to live."

The kids turned their heads.

I turned mine.

A thin stream of cigarette smoke drifted upward
as he continued:

"When a Yimugi—an immature dragon—
endures for a thousand years,
it finally rises to the sky.

That one waited 999 years,
held everything in...

but on the very last year,
our little rascals were running around under the tree,
screaming and thumping and shaking the earth."

The kids froze.

One swallowed loudly.

The uncle nodded slowly.

"So that Yimugi, one day before ascension,
lost its temper.

It snapped.

It was ready for revenge."

Then he glanced at me
with a strangely serious face.

"...But kids, listen well.

On the night Dong-gi was born—
that very night—
a bolt of lightning struck
and hit the Yimugi straight in the head.

That's why it never made it to the sky.

It's still hiding somewhere."

"Ehhh~~ Who would believe that?!"
the kids cried.

The uncle pointed with his chin.

"Look under that zelkova.
See that dark scorch mark?

That's the lightning scar.

And Dong-gi?
He's Admiral Yi Sun-sin reborn.

Haven't you heard the village stories?"

"My mom said that too!" a kid shouted.

"She said Dong-gi-hyeong is the Admiral's reincarnation!"

I groaned.

"Uncles, what are you teaching these kids...?

Come on—General.
CHECKMATE. Game over."

The uncles burst into laughter.

Then one of them added:

"You see him beating all of us at janggi?
That's the Admiral's strategy right there."

Another nodded seriously.

"Right now, Dong-gi is living here,
so the Yimugi is too scared to come out.

But if you kids keep causing trouble...

Dong-gi might get tired and move away.

Then the Yimugi will come back for revenge.

No one will be able to stop it.

So don't mess around near that zelkova tree.
Got it?"

The kids nodded, eyes wide.

And me?

I sat there thinking:

I wasn't doing anything...
and somehow a whole myth
formed around me.

That evening, walking home
under the early dusk,
I passed the zelkova tree again.

A wind brushed past my ear—
soft, cold,
and strangely watchful.

For a moment—just one moment—
I wondered:

Maybe the adults were right.

Maybe I really did strike
something ancient,
and coiled,
and waiting.

Because in my village,
grown-ups never scolded children directly.

They taught with stories—
quiet stories,
half-jokes, half-warnings,
the kind that slip into a child's heart
before he even knows it.

And so, without my knowing,
my own birth-legends
had been wandering through the village
for years and years—

little myths carried by the wind,
told under the eaves,
whispered at dusk—

until even I began to wonder
which parts were true,
and which parts were simply love.

chapters.title: Scene 10 - Judgement
chapters.content:
A few days later, the ghost community held a baseball match.

And that idiot Messenger...

he went and punched a ghost from another village.

The Dokkaebi came running to me, pale as rice paper.

"General...! W-we're doomed...!

The Messenger hit a foreign ghost...

They dragged him to King Yeomra's court...!"

I pressed my fingers against my forehead.

"This punk... seriously..."

So of course,
I was summoned to the Underworld Court.

King Yeomra sat high on the judgment seat.

Grim reapers lined up on both sides.

And the Messenger knelt on the floor, shaking like wet laundry.

"Why did you hit her?" King Yeomra asked.

The Messenger stammered so hard his voice cracked.

"T-there was a crying child-ghost over there...

so... I hit his mother ghost..."

The entire court buzzed.

"What does a crying kid...

have to do with punching his mom?"

The Messenger trembled even harder
and pointed at me.

"O-our Boss...

whenever his friend's younger brother cried...

he would hit the older brother.

A-and the crying always stopped...

So... I used the same... strategy..."

King Yeomra stared at me, half speechless.

"You.

You must have a reason. Right?"

I stepped forward
and bowed deeply at the center of the courtroom.

"Your Majesty,

I lived with those village kids
like real brothers.

We ate together,
did homework together,
slept in each other's homes,
and I treated their parents with respect.

And their parents
treated me like a son.

That is what 'neighbors as family' means in my village.

But this foolish Messenger
copied only the surface
of what he saw.


That is my failure.
I taught him wrong."

Then I turned, kneeled,
and bowed to the ghost he had hit.

"I apologize first.

The fault is mine."

The ghost flailed his hands in panic.

"Oh, General! What sin could you possibly have?!

You mustn't lower yourself like this!

You saved us in the war
four hundred years ago...

How could we resent you?

Please, rise. We understand everything."

I slowly stood up
and spoke quietly.


"But the Messenger still committed a sin.

And he must face judgment."

The courtroom fell dead silent.

Even the Dokkaebi swallowed hard.

✦ The Sentence

"By law,
the Messenger deserves
one hundred years in the flaming cauldron.

But—

if Your Majesty
and the victim here
grant mercy...

then strip him of his Messenger rank
and place him under
my Servant Duty Command."

King Yeomra frowned.

"You... need a servant?"

"No, Your Majesty.

Just reincarnate him as a dog.

I will personally teach him
how to read context—

front, back, above, below,
the whole cause-and-effect of life."

King Yeomra turned to the Messenger.

"Messenger.

Will you take the cauldron?

Or will you become their dog?"

The Messenger burst into tears.

"I-I will live as a dog!

I will learn from the General...!"

King Yeomra raised his hand.

"Then hear my judgment.

The Messenger is hereby stripped of rank,
reincarnated into the human world,
and ordered to serve as Dong-gi's dog
for ten years!"

"Thank you, Your Majesty.

Now... before we send him down...

shall we have a cup of tea?"

✦ The Dog Arrives

The next morning,
my wife somehow brought home
a small puppy
and even built him a little house.

I crouched down,
looked the dog straight in the eyes,
and muttered:

"You nearly died yesterday,
you Son of—"

The puppy wagged its tail
as if it understood everything
and nothing
at the same time.

I sighed
and patted its head.

"Alright.

Let's start your training.

The human world is much tougher
than the underworld."

chapters.title: Scene 1 - Flower Garden Village
chapters.content:
Flower Garden Village

Flower Garden Village earned its name because,

when spring came, the mountains turned into a sea of color—

purple blossoms, pink azaleas,

and white apple flowers covering the slopes like a soft, bright veil.

On the morning of Seollal, the Lunar New Year,

our whole family dressed in our best hanbok

and made our way to Flower Garden Village.

My father was the youngest among his brothers,

and since all my uncles had already passed away,

we were to hold the ancestral rites

at the home of my eldest cousin—

the first son of my late eldest uncle.

The air that morning was cold,

and the dew on the grass soaked the cuffs of my pants,

but still we had to follow the mountain path

stretching far into the distance.

When we arrived at my cousin's home,

his wife would come out to greet us

and guide us into the warm anbang.

My cousin, as the eldest son of the senior line,

was already in the kitchen—

preparing the dishes for the ancestral rites.

In our family,

it was the men—especially the heir—

who took charge of the ritual food.

It may sound unusual to others,

but it followed the same tradition

that existed in the royal court of Joseon,

where the king's meals were prepared

not by women,

but by specially appointed male cooks

who held both authority and responsibility.

So in our house,

the kitchen during ancestral rites

was not a women's space

but an extension of the family's law—

a tradition inherited like a crown.

Before the table could be set,

the younger children were given small tasks.

We cracked walnuts with a hammer or a stone mill,

often bruising the kernels.

Then the older cousins would shake their heads and say,

"You're still too young—

your hands don't have enough strength."

And they would show us

how to open a walnut with bare hands,

splitting the shell cleanly

and lifting out the kernel

without a single scratch.

Watching that sort of skill—

quiet, steady, precise—

we couldn't help but admire them.

It was the moment when a child

first understood

the dignity carried in a man's hands.

As our family lived through

the Imjin War against Japan

and the Manchu War,

many of the older men were lost,

and the old laws and traditions

vanished with them.

In that emptiness,

people who had never been nobles

began imitating the customs

of households where the men had died—

traditions reduced to nothing

but their outer shell.

But our family was one of the few

that still remembered the old ways.

My cousin preparing the ritual dishes himself

was one of the last traces

of that fading order.

Morning light slid across the wooden floor,

and the house seemed to hold its breath—

as if it knew a ritual was about to begin.

When the ancestral rite began,

we lined up according to our hangnyeol—

our place in the family line—

and bowed in turn.

Then we stepped out of the room,

leaving the space quiet

so the ancestors could "take their meal."

For ten, maybe twenty minutes,

we waited in the cold hallway,

breath faint in the air,

until it was time to return.

When we went back inside,

we extinguished the incense

and started clearing the dishes.

My cousin would turn to my father and ask,

"How should we do the eumbok, Uncle?"

And my father would answer,

firm but gentle:

"Just touch the cup with your lips.

You've got friends to meet later,

and you need to visit your in-laws too.

Drinking and driving—

that's the quickest way

to ruin a man's life."

And just like that,

the room shifted back into the world of the living—

steam fading from the dishes,

footsteps softening,

the weight of tradition settling quietly

into the corners of the house.

Afterward, we set up two large tables for the meal—

one for the men,

and one for the women.

It wasn't about hierarchy,

or distance,

or formality.

It was simply a way

to avoid any misunderstanding

that might arise

from physical closeness—

even among family.

I had heard the old saying,

"romance happens under the dining table,"

so I understood the idea—

but I never imagined it could happen

within a family.

That part always puzzled me.

After the meal,

we usually had a small dessert time.

We mostly ate apples—

and even my older sister

had to peel them.

The older cousins would tease her,

half joking, half teaching:

"Goodness, if you peel an apple that thick,

there'll be nothing left to eat!"

Then they would take the knife themselves

and show her how to do it properly.

Their blade moved in one unbroken line,

and the peel came off

thinner than a sheet of tissue—

smooth, clean,

like they were slicing wind.

The moment my father picked up

the apple my sister had peeled,

a thought flashed through my mind:

The older cousins have made a mistake.

And sure enough,

my father spoke in a calm, steady voice:

"Now that our Dong-gi is married,

he should start learning

how to manage the logistics.

And you—

our new bride—

you should learn it as well."

And watching him,

I understood something for the first time—

that this is how power is used.

And that moment taught me something else—

something darker,

something I had felt for years

but never had the words for.

In our family,

a single mistake

didn't end with a scolding

or a laugh.

It awakened

a quiet, unseen law—

a force that needed no shouting,

no threats,

only a single sentence

from the right person

to shift the entire room.

That was why I hated

going to Jeongja Village.

Because behind the laughter,

behind the warm greetings,

behind the trays of food,

there was always that silent rule:

one mistake,

and the weight of the whole family

could fall on you.

And as a child—

a child standing at the lowest step

of a powerful lineage—

I felt that weight more sharply

than anyone knew.

I drank the sujeonggwa — a cinnamon-ginger drink with a hint of dried persimmon my mother made

and fell asleep like a child.

When I woke up in the evening,

my wife was sitting beside me,

quietly watching over me.

I said to her,

"Nuna..."

—a Korean way of addressing an older woman,

even when she is your wife—

"you're lucky, you know.

You never had to endure

the hardships of a daughter-in-law."

"In a family like ours," I added,

"being a daughter-in-law isn't minor league.

It's more like...

World Series level."

"I'm sorry," I said.

"I think I got called up today.

Looks like...

we're both major leaguers now."

My wife laughed softly and said,

"Well...

I guess I really did marry

into the right family."

The next morning, my wife and I went to the stream and skated on the ice. My wife was clumsy at first and fell several times, but as I taught her to bend her knees, lean forward, and pull herself along, she quickly got the hang of it. The natural ice rink—something no city could offer—was ours alone.

Exhausted from the cold, we returned home and spent the last hours of Lunar New Year by the brazier, roasting sweet potatoes, chatting softly, and enjoying the warmth together.

chapters.title: Scene 2 - The First Full Moon of the Lunar Year
chapters.content:
Fifteen days after Lunar New Year, Koreans celebrate the First Full Moon called 'Daeborem'.

People crack nuts to wish for strong teeth

and light fires along the field edges

to chase away pests

and invite good fortune for the year.

I was eating peanuts with my family

when a Dokkaebi called me from outside.

I stepped out and asked,

"What's going on?"

The Dokkaebi announced,

"Your puppy—Messenger—is getting married!"

I laughed softly.

"That rascal... he works fast."

The Dokkaebi tilted his head.

"Do you know who he's marrying?"

I replied,

"The widow ghost whose kid he punched last time."

He blinked hard.

"How do you know that?"

I smiled like someone hiding a secret.

"That was one of my pictures."

"What picture?" he asked.

I shrugged.

"If Messenger gets married, maybe he'll finally grow up."

The Dokkaebi frowned.

"But... how on earth did you manage to get a puppy married?"

I answered calmly,

"When I went to the Underworld,

I learned the ghost he assaulted

was a widow ghost raising a kid alone.

Human or ghost—raising a child alone is never easy."

The Dokkaebi nodded.

"True enough..."

I continued,

"Still, Messenger hit her.

He had to be punished.

But punishment that hurts both sides?

What good is that?

So I nudged the verdict

so both of them could walk away with something."

He leaned in.

"But... did Messenger accept it?"

I shook my head.

**"Of course not.

His pride is too big.

He would've refused for sure.

So I thought,

'Well... if he lives as a puppy for a while,

he'll learn his place.'

That's why I turned him into a dog."**

The Dokkaebi just stared.

"...And that led to marriage?"

I smiled slyly.

"After the verdict, I had tea with King Yeomna.

We made a small wager.

'I bet they'll marry within a year.'

That's what I told him."

The Dokkaebi murmured,

"But shouldn't they love each other first?"

I nodded.

"Exactly.

So I gave them a gentle path to walk together."

The Steps

Step 1:

Medicine for her wounds—quietly—

with the dog delivering the message:

This is from him.

Step 2:

Strawberry-flavored candies for her child,

again delivered by the dog,

again in my name.

Step 3:

I ordered the dog to watch over her child.

Message:

For your kid.

Step 4:

Then I sent him again—

not with gifts this time,

but with time, laughter, and play.

Message shifting slightly:

For your cute kid.

Step 5:

And then... every day,

I sent the dog again.

Until one day she looked at him and asked,

half laughing, half shy:

"You again... for my kid?"

That was the moment I had been waiting for.

And the Messenger—

using every ounce of courage,

just as I'd trained him—

whispered softly:

"Not for your kid.

Only for you."


The Dokkaebi scratched his head.

"So... then what happened?"

I sighed

and looked at him for a long moment.

**"That," I said,

"is exactly why you can't get married.

If someone shows up every day,

cares for her child,

brings warmth into her home—

tell me,

what woman—or ghost—

wouldn't eventually open her heart?"**

The Dokkaebi's eyes brightened.

"Then... can I get married too?"

I rubbed my forehead.

"Fine. Who's your type?"

He blushed—

yes, a blushing Dokkaebi—

and stammered,

"There's this beautiful woman on your television...

the one who turns the letters...

'R', 'S', 'T', 'L', 'N', 'E'...

the English word game..."

I froze.

Stared.

Then smacked the back of his head.

"Vanna White!!!

From Wheel of Fortune!

On AFKN!!

Oh my God!"

The Dokkaebi rubbed his head,

eyes watery.

"...She's really pretty though..."


And as the cold air of Daeboreum wrapped around us,

I thought:

Maybe the First Full Moon Day

is nothing more

and nothing less

than a wish for a year

filled with health

and quiet happiness.

chapters.title: Scene 3 - Messenger's wife
chapters.content:
A few days later,

the Messenger showed up at my house with his new wife in tow.

I crossed my arms.

Me:

"Messenger!!

You're more capable than I thought!"

Messenger:

"Heh-heh...

It's all thanks to you, my lord.

I got a beautiful wife and a lovely son—

all at once!"

Me:

"Good.

Now live well.

You're an adult now—

you've got mouths to feed."

His wife dropped to her knees and bowed deeply.

Me:

"Hey—hey—what's with the big bow?"

Messenger's Wife:

"General...

You saved us both in the old war centuries ago...

and now you've given me a new husband as well.

I will never forget this grace."

Me:

"Grace!

Too much!!!

Anyway!"

I pointed at the Messenger.

Me:

"From today,

you're no longer just some wandering ghost.

You're officially a Messenger again.

Which means—

you're eligible for the traineeship program."

Messenger blinked hard.

Me:

"Traineeship.

Go spend some time in Odin's Kingdom—

learn the language, the customs...

You know, officially.

Even the King of Death is improving employee benefits these days"

Messenger:

"Th-then what about me?"

Me:

"You?

Go on your honeymoon first.

A week.

Enjoy it.

Then report back."

Just then,

Dokkaebi popped in from the corner like a nosy uncle.

Dokkaebi:

"Uh... General?

What about me?

Do I get anything?"

I looked at him like he asked for a Ferrari.

Me:

"You?

Go watch TV.

There are plenty of pretty ghost ladies around—

and you still can't even talk to one properly?!

Sort yourself out first!"

Dokkaebi drooped like wet laundry.

The Messenger stood there glowing with pride,

his wife shyly clinging to his sleeve,

the whole ghost community finally settling into peace.

chapters.title: Scene 4 - Kimchi-Mandu
chapters.content:
Korea's kimjang season—late autumn—was nothing short of a battlefield against napa cabbage. Adults moved like winter soldiers, sleeves rolled up, hands reddened from salt and icy water.

I still remember that sight: people rinsing mountains of salted cabbage along the riverside, their boots sinking into the mud, steam rising from their breath in the sharp air.

Sometimes, as if it were the most natural thing in the world, they loaded five hundred heads of napa cabbage onto a Kyeong-un-gi— that rattling village tractor— and hauled it down the dirt road like a small parade of winter preparations.

My mother was from Seoul, so she wanted to add jeotgal (salted seafood) and fresh oysters to our kimchi. But once— I ate it and threw up, then spent the whole night running to the outhouse. After that, she used only the clean, simple ingredients that came straight from our mountain village.

After washing the napa cabbages in a big rubber tub— the kind a child could almost bathe in— she sprinkled a mountain of salt over them to soften the leaves. Then she rinsed them clean and stacked the cabbages in the yard, building a small wall of winter work.

For the kimchi-so— the mixture of sliced Korean radish, red chili pepper, garlic, green onions, and all the other seasonings— my mother and the village ladies packed it gently between every layer of napa cabbage leaves, filling even the smallest empty spaces.

Then they lowered the cabbages into a traditional earthenware jar— an onggi breathing quietly in the cold air. She cut radish into big, chunky pieces and tucked them in as well, so everything could ferment together and share the same winter sleep.

There was another kind of kimchi— dongchimi, the clear, cold water-kimchi of winter. My mother never added seasonings to it. She simply poured water and salt into an earthenware jar, added the rinsed cabbages, big chunks of radish, and even the radish leaves, letting them settle quietly in the cold brine. She never buried the jar underground; the winter itself—cold as an ice castle— was more than enough to ferment everything.

After about a month, the kimchi was fully ripened— fermented to its clear, clean depth. It wasn't spicy at all. It tasted of the napa cabbage's quiet sweetness with that crisp, icy snap when you bit into it.

We didn't need anything else. Just sliced kimchi, a bowl of dongchimi, and steaming hot rice— a whole meal, simple and perfect.

I especially loved kimchi-mandu.

One day between Lunar New Year and Daeboreum, our aunts and older sisters gathered at our house like migrating birds.

The sisters dusted flour over a big wooden board and rolled out the dough with a heavy wooden club— shaped almost like an old laundry mallet— flattening it into thin, round mandu skins.

The aunts sat beside them, filling each wrapper with mandu mixture, pinching the edges tight so none would burst later. They teased, "If your mandu doesn't burst, you'll have pretty babies when you get married!"

At that, my sisters shaped their dumplings with the soul of true artists. I tried to follow along, but secretly pinched the dumpling that Seonju-nuna had made— just enough to leave a tiny wound.

When the pile reached a hundred, my mother began boiling water in the huge steamer. When it reached two hundred, she spread a hemp steaming cloth, stood up a full layer of mandu, then another cloth, another layer— stacking ten levels high like a tower of winter blessings.

I waited for the mandu to finish steaming... and somewhere along the way, I fell asleep.

The next morning, my mother brought out a huge bamboo tray piled high with freshly steamed mandu. All the women who had helped make them gathered around me, their eyes bright with mischief.

"Well? Which one is the prettiest?" they asked, watching where my hand would go.

I grinned. "Good grief... am I supposed to marry everyone here? Look at these! Every single one of them burst open! This one blew out its left side— that one blew out its right. And this one... look at that little mouth sticking out— just like my wife when she's mad!"

Beside me, my mother clapped along, "Look at you!" keeping time like it was a small festival.

When I finally picked the prettiest mandu in the whole tray, she gave me a soft, proud smile— one only a mother can make.

I popped a dumpling into my mouth. "Well then— I guess I'll have to spend my whole life with the lady who made this one!"

The aunts burst into laughter. "Dong-gi! Then you'll be living with your mother forever!"

I answered, "Of course I'll live with my mom. But I guess I'll have to live with the one who made that dumpling with the little mouth poking out too... though I'm scared our baby might turn out crooked!"

The aunts roared with laughter, and just like that, our First Full Moon Day morning began.

By the way, our family's steamed mandu had a special signature. We rinsed the kimchi clean, then mixed it with pork, tofu, and a touch of black pepper. The taste landed somewhere between a meat dumpling and a kimchi dumpling— light, clean, never tiring, with the crisp texture of kimchi still alive in every bite.

Epilogue

That evening, Seonju-nuna brought out a plate of mandu, still sulking. "Hey, husband! Find the one I made!"

"What? How am I supposed to find that? A dumpling isn't a person!"

"You said mine was ugly— the one with the little mouth sticking out!" she cried.

"Come on now... even a grumpy, lopsided dumpling looks beautiful when it's made by someone as pretty as you."

I picked up the dumpling with my fingernail mark and popped it into my mouth.

She sighed— not quite defeat, but that soft kind of surrender only someone close can give.

"I'm a barbie girl trapped in your palm... ain't I? I'm yours, boy." she muttered, and quietly began eating her dumplings.

My mother set aside a few mandu as an offering—
a quiet wish for peace in the house,
warm relationships,
and the kind of comfort only a good meal can bring.

chapters.title: Scene 5 - The Realm of Women (ft. Liam Neeson)
chapters.content:
Winter in the countryside had a strange kind of quiet—a quiet that settled not only on the frozen fields but on the lives of the people who worked them. It was the slack season, the long breath after harvest, when farmers waited for spring like a letter that never arrived.

In the 1980s and early 1990s, some elders still remembered the hunger of the old days, but with the arrival of Tongil-byeo rice, a little comfort finally entered our bowls. We were not rich—just no longer starving. Sometimes, that alone felt like a miracle.

On winter nights, the village women gathered at our house. My mother was gifted at knitting, so the others came to learn—carrying balls of yarn, knitting needles, and small bundles of snacks. They began with knitting, but soon the stories spilled out—housework, family matters, and the kind of secret romances a kid like me had no business knowing.

I lay on my stomach peeling tangerines, pretending to do homework. My motto was always the same: "I know nothing." If I ever asked, "Mom, what does that mean?" the whole room would freeze over, and the adventure would end right there. So I kept my mouth shut and my ears wide open.

That night, Gyu-hak's mother began first. (The main cast: Gyu-hak's mom, Changho's mom, Seonju-nuna, and my own mother—the elite squad of Eunpunggol's knitting brigade.)

"My hometown is deep in the mountains of Gangwon-do," she said. "When we played at a friend's house at night, there was this boy who always walked me home. Back then I didn't understand anything. If he liked me, he should've grabbed my hand or at least tried to sneak a kiss! But he just walked beside me like a tree stump. So my first love floated away across the water."

The women burst into laughter.

"That's right! Boys need to do something for a girl to know!"

Then Changho's mother chimed in: "No, no! We girls have to make a move too!" And she dove into her own story.

"When I took Changho's father to meet my dad, my dad wouldn't even accept his greeting. Didn't like him one bit. I thought it was over—so I packed my clothes and whatever little money I had and ran away to Ulleungdo. Changho's father panicked and followed me."

She clicked her tongue.

"During the Korean War he marched all the way to the Yalu River (Amnok-gang)—believing the country was finally about to be reunified—but then the Chinese army pushed back. People said he took down a thousand men in that retreat. When Changho's father heard that story, his legs shook like noodles. Said he almost wet himself when my father looked at him once—just once."

They howled with laughter.

"In Ulleungdo we tried to live quietly. I sent my father an apology letter—didn't even write the address. But he found us anyway, dragged his old army buddies along, and crossed the sea like a general chasing deserters. I thought I was going to die."

"And then," she said, "he saw my belly—and said to Changho's father, 'Live well,' and left."

Later she asked how he tracked them down. "Apparently he saw the word 'Ulleungdo' on the postage stamp and mobilized every old comrade he had. Came with a military knife on his belt—

but when he saw Changho's father stepping off the squid boat at dawn, exhausted from working through the night with me,

he decided, 'At least the boy takes responsibility.'

He always said a child—his daughter—is scarier than a thousand enemy soldiers.

And he wasn't wrong"

More laughter exploded. "In war or peace, someone's gotta make one—am I wrong?" They jabbed Seonju-nuna. "So? You making anything yet?"

Seonju puffed her cheeks. "I need something sweet... heavenly sweet..." The women shrieked with laughter and all eyes landed on me.

"Dong-gi! Give Seonju some heaven-sweetness!"

I answered, stone-faced: "Heaven-sweet? Too easy. I've got a hundred honeypots in my warehouse."

They collapsed.

When the night was over and everyone went home, I asked Seonju quietly:

"But... how do you make one?"

She tilted her head and whispered, "Your mother says you've got ten foxes and twenty snakes living inside your belly."

"...So that helps you make one?"

Then she lowered her voice, half playful, half shy: "My lord... I admit defeat tonight. Please spare me."

She pulled the blanket over her shoulder and turned her back to me.

I thought, "It's too early for all this. If I ever have a baby, I guess I'll have to raise it on my own... since my parents won't be any help."

That's just how boys were in my village—your child is yours to raise. No excuses.

All of a sudden, I remembered what Changho's mother once said:

"My father used to say that one of his old war comrades—the one who somehow washed up on Ulleungdo with him—was an American soldier named Liam Neeson. Maybe it was just someone with the same name... but raising a daughter? That man must've lived through a war of his own."

Back then, fathers were brave. But daughters—daughters were even braver.

---

chapters.title: Scene 6 - Letter from Odin's Kingdom 1
chapters.content:
Since last Lunar New Year,
I had work to do
alongside my wife.

No matter how young a child was,
they had their share
of household work.

Leading the ox out to graze,
picking mulberry leaves
for the silkworms—

at the very least,
cooking rice at home
was a child's duty.

That was how
we learned to live.
With our hands.
Day by day.

That day,

a letter had arrived
from the Kingdom of Odin.



To my Lord,

Thanks to you, I am studying well here in the northern lands of Odin's Kingdom. During the day, I learn ghost-welfare studies, and I even take computer classes—typing with fingers that were invisible for five hundred years.
