But... when the school bell rings, everyone goes straight home. No one walks outside. No one gathers. No one laughs in the streets.

Back in Eunpunggol, we played baseball at Songjeong, the ladies chatted and teased each other, we steamed potatoes and corn, and cooked ramyeon together on cold nights.

Here... nothing like that exists.

And even if a ghost wanders out at night and gets into an accident, the other ghosts only say, 'Well, you should've been more careful!' No comfort, no warmth—just cold northern common sense.

The evenings are so quiet that even the wind feels lonely.

I will study hard, finish the program early, and return as soon as I can.

I promise to devote myself to building the ghost-welfare world you envisioned.

Sincerely yours,

Your devoted trainee

chapters.title: Scene 7 - Madam Chungju
chapters.content:
I didn't know Madam Chungju very well,

but she had known my mother
long before I was even born.

She once lived in Seoul,
but moved to our village.

And from that day on,
whenever my mother had to leave home,
she called only one person.

Madam Chungju.

When the busy farming season ended,
and winter touched the edge of the village,

my mother often went on long trips
with the other village ladies.

They would charter a bus—
that was the fashionable word back then—

and even order matching outfits
from the shops in town.

It was their way
of easing the exhaustion
left behind by the burning summer.

They traveled across famous places,
as if gathering back
the pieces of themselves
they had given to their families.

One day,
before leaving on a two-night, three-day trip,
my mother told her:

"Please keep an eye on Dong-gi.

And if anyone knocks—
anyone you don't know—

don't open the door."

Then she left with her travel bag,
the women's chatter fading down the road
like migrating birds.

On the third day,
I waited for her return.

Somewhere along the way,
I fell asleep.

The next morning,
when I opened my eyes,

the whole room looked like
an 80s souvenir shop.

Travel guidebooks.
Trinkets stacked like mountains.

And toys—so many toys.

A miniature Bulguksa pagoda.
A kaleidoscope of temple slides.
A wooden turtle ship
of Admiral Yi Sun-sin.

All of it sitting in our storage room
like treasures from a faraway carnival.

That evening, during dinner
with my mother,
Madam Chungju,
and Seonju-nuna,

my mother suddenly turned to her.

"You big silly Teddy bear of mine..."

Madam Chungju waved both hands.

"Oh my goodness, sister~~
please don't say it like that..."

I stared.

"What?
What happened yesterday?"

Seonju-nuna answered first.

"Last night!
Mom came home and knocked,

but Auntie here
wouldn't open the door!"

Madam Chungju lifted her chin proudly.

"No matter how I listened,
it did NOT sound like your mother's voice!

And before she left,
she told me—

'Don't open for strangers.'

So I locked it tighter!"

I gasped.

"Mom!
Then what did YOU do?"

My mother slapped her thigh.

"What else!

I walked straight to the church
and begged them
to let me sleep there for the night!"

Later, we heard what Madam Chungju
had whispered to Seonju-nuna.

"Lock the door tight!

There's some flower-headed crazy woman outside yelling,
'Open up! Open the door!'

If anything happens,
carry Dong-gi on your back
and run home at once!"

My mother nearly choked.

"You silly Teddy woman!

Try shouting and singing
for two whole days—

of course my voice
wouldn't sound normal!"

Madam Chungju,
hurt in the most innocent way,
murmured:

"I only did
exactly what you told me..."

That was it.

Seonju-nuna and I burst into laughter.

Rolling on the floor.
Holding our stomachs.
Tears streaming down our faces.

While my mother clicked her tongue,
half angry,
half amused.

Madam Chungju was that kind of woman.

Steady.
Loyal.
Stubborn
in the sweetest way.

And from that day on,
whenever my mother had to leave home,
she always said with a laugh:

"Lock the door tight, you hear?

Just like that night."

chapters.title: Scene 8 - Dokkaebi's Another one
chapters.content:
I called the Messenger over.

Me:

"Hey—where's that these days?

He vanished off the face of the earth.

What now—still sulking because you got married?"

Messenger (trying not to explode laughing):

"Well... he fell in love again."

Me:

"Again??
First it was BANANA—OOPS! Vana White...
Who is it this time?
Who's the unlucky victim this round?"

Messenger straightened up like he was reporting to a general.

Messenger:

"Winter Tinkerbell, sir!"

I stared.

Me:

"...What the hell. From where—Germany?"

Messenger nodded with heroic pride.

Messenger:

"Yes, sir. Exactly."

I slapped my forehead so hard my soul left my body.

Me:

"Oh my God—Katarina Witt!!!

Tell that idiot this:

NO more TV shows.

None. Zero. Gone.

If he falls in love one more time,

I'll kill him myself."

chapters.title: Scene 9 - Miss Catherine
chapters.content:
One day, Miss Catherine—my cat—ate a piece of sausage laced with poison and died.

That rascal...

Whenever I ate sausage, I scolded her once or twice,

so she would pretend she didn't care for it at all.

But the moment I went off to school,

she must have taken the poisoned bait.

Looking back,

the fact that she held herself back in front of me—

as if she had her own pride—

feels strangely noble.


Sometimes I still miss her.

Miss Catherine, who survived on the leftovers from my bowl.

I miss gathering her into my arms,

listening to her soft little grrrr~,

pressing my thumb against her warm jelly-paws—

soft as a tiny Haribo,

warm as a living thing that trusted me too much.

When she first came into our home,

I took her with me to the stream where I washed my hair.

I covered her in shampoo

and dunked her straight into the water.

She must have screamed inside her tiny cat brain:

"I've met the wrong human..."

Epilogue — Now Miss Catherine Can Finally Speak

The day I first arrived at this house,

a tiny human I had never seen before

tried to scoop me up without so much as a greeting.

How rude.

So I slipped under the wardrobe and hid.

But then—

the scent of sausage.

Sweet. Warm. Fatal.

It dragged me out like a spell.

Before I knew it,

the tiny human was already at the stream,

covered head to toe in bubbles, shampooing away.

And then—

I realized with a jolt:

"Wrong house.

I've come to the wrong house.

Wait... am I a 'Bubble Cat' now?"

Cold water hit my back.

I kicked and thrashed.

But the tiny human pinned me down and scolded:

"Stay still!

Who told you to roll around in dust holes?

Dust ball cannot enter my room!"

Not the big human,

not the other tiny humans—

no one scolded him.

And at that moment,

a subtitle flashed across my feline brain:

"If only I were better at catching mice...

I wouldn't be suffering like this.

But one thing is clear—

this tiny human controls my food bowl."

After my fur finally dried,

I climbed onto his lap

and sang my soft 'grrrr-song'.

He gave me a piece of sausage—

a good one.

And stared at me with that unmistakable

'You're adorable...' look.

"...Fine.

Yes. I probably did meet the wrong human.

But still—

my human...

is this tiny one."

To Miss Catherine

I never gave you the name "Butterfly."

People call caterpillars filthy pests,

then worship butterflies as if they were holy.

I refused to let that foolish contradiction

becarved into your name as well.

chapters.title: Scene 10 - Rumor Travels Faster Than Light
chapters.content:
No one remembered who started it—
but before my mother and Seonju-nuna even returned from the clinic,
the rumor had already run a full lap around the village:

"Little Groom broke a chamber pot!"
"No, not a pot— a cast-iron lid blasted into the sky!"
"I heard the kid... made another kid!"

Stories fluttered between the wash-place, the market,
and the jars at the jangdokdae,
traveling faster than any kind of light ever could.

One afternoon, while I wasn't home,

my mother and Seonju-nuna headed down to the wash-place.

The village ladies had rolled their baggy pants above the knee,
settled themselves on flat river stones,
and were beating laundry with their paddles—
thwak, thwak, thwak.

Changho's mother said, loud enough for Volga River sailors to hear,
lips curled into a needle-sharp grin:

"Good grief... Changho's daddy can't even punch through wet paper."

She smacked her laundry twice as hard for emphasis.

Chungju's aunt shot back,
"Paper? What paper?
I don't even have a husband to show the heavens to!"

Then Jungho's mother added,
"I heard the pot lid really DID fly into the sky that night!"

The wash-place roared.

Changho's mother pointed her paddle at Seonju-nuna.

"Where did Dong-gi learn stuff like that, huh?"

Seonju rolled her eyes.

"You all taught him! Why ask me?"

Every auntie fired back at once:

"What did we ever teach him?!"

Seonju sighed like a K-drama lead forced into a nonsense scene.

"Last winter—
you all were sewing at our house.
You talked about everything.

And my husband heard every word."

Silence.
The aunties froze.

"But that day," one protested,

"we told him to 'show the heavens,'
and he didn't know a thing!"

Seonju clicked her tongue.

"He wasn't clueless.
He was pretending.

He told me:
'If I interrupt the grown-up fun talk,
they'll stop telling the juicy parts.

Why overturn a feast someone lovingly set?'
So he stayed quiet."

The aunties gasped and wailed:

"That brat! Ten snakes curled in his belly!"
"We were monkeys dancing in his palm!"
"I told you! That boy isn't normal—be careful!"


Just then, I happened to walk past the wash-place.

Chungju's aunt waved me over.

"Dong-gi!
Where did you show Seonju the heaven-sweetness?!"

So I stepped onto a flat stone,
said nothing,
pulled down my pants,
and cast a golden arc into the stream
like James Dean in Giants film making.

"Is this strong enough

to send a pot lid flying to heaven?"

The wash-place exploded.

"He's eaten every auntie in this village alive!"

I sat on the biggest stone and announced:

"They say kid's pee is good medicine.
Your hands will get prettier, aunties~"

The laughter doubled—
until Chungju's aunt slipped
and nearly tumbled into the water.


I pointed at Changho's mother:

"Auntie, you look refreshed.
Take another honeymoon to Ulleungdo—
just like 30 years ago."

The auntie beside her giggled.
I pointed at her too.

"And you—

feed your husband some oysters.
I heard he's running low on power."

The wash-place howled.

And then my mother appeared.

"Aigo~~ Mrs. Kim!
Please control your boy!
He's embarrassing us!"

My mother shook her head.
Laughed silently once.
And then—
her face iced over like winter glass.

"You folks can laugh.
I laughed too.

But listen.

The day they brought Seonju home—
you all saw it.
Dong-gi walked out with a knife.

This isn't a mother bragging.
When that boy's eyes roll back,
no one can stop him.

And now he has a child.
If I try to stop him,
he'll turn into a bronze demon—
and blood will spill.

So stop.
No more talk.
No more jokes.

Before the whole village becomes a disgrace—
zip your lips.

I may be smiling,
but I'm not smiling."

The laughter collapsed like a tent in the rain.

Jungho's mother whispered,

"If my husband treasured me
even half as much as Dong-gi treasures Seonju,
I'd follow him like Jesus..."

After that day,

nobody in Eunpunggol mentioned the pregnancy again.

But something else began.

The meals.

Without a word exchanged,
the village's menu shifted—
as if they had all quietly signed
a secret culinary pact.

Breakfast: fried oysters.
Lunch: baked oysters.
Dinner... oyster hot dogs.

It was like the whole village had decided
to rebuild a man from the inside out.

No comments.
No winks.
Just oysters sliding onto plates
like some coastal American medicine
the aunties discovered overnight.

I asked Seonju:

"Why did you go to the hospital...?"

She answered sweetly:

"Mom and I had a health checkup~"

Butthe oysters kept coming—
andeveryone kept watching me
withthat strange grown-up look—
theone they give you
whenthey'repreparing you
fora destiny too embarrassing
tosay out loud.

chapters.title: Scene 1 - Duplicator
chapters.content:
It was late afternoon, sometime in my third year of elementary school,
the sun already slanting toward the hills.
I went to the schoolyard with my older sister
and a few of her friends, just to pass the time.


Near the sink, beside the art room,
our homeroom teacher was pulling open a large drawer.

From inside emerged, one by one:
a dark blue ink container,
a rubber roller,
and a square wooden frame.


The class president stood next to him,
and the air carried the unmistakable feeling
that something important was about to happen.


We couldn't contain our curiosity
and ran straight over.

"Teacher, what are you doing?"

"I'm printing the test papers.

Wanna help?"


Before he even finished the sentence,
we shouted back in unison,

"Yes~~!"



The teacher stretched the paraffin sheet tight
across the mimeograph frame—
a thing that looked like a construction-site sand sieve.


My older sister rolled the ink onto the board,
feeding the rubber roller until it shone dark and wet.
I carefully slid the thin test paper
under the frame, one sheet at a time.


Then the teacher pushed the roller—
shhk—


and on the rough, gray paper,
crooked, pale letters slowly appeared.


The smell of ink stabbed my nose,
but I didn't mind it at all.
Inside that smell was the feeling
that we were doing something important.


We printed sixty sheets.
Not a single one of us complained.



Printing the test papers took only a moment,
but writing the questions for them
took days.


The teacher would place the paraffin sheet
on a metal plate
and, with a pen that released no ink,
carve each question line by line into the surface.


Watching that, I thought to myself,
There's no way I could ever be a schoolteacher...
I already hated dictation as it was.


When test day came,
cries erupted from every corner of the classroom.

"Teacher, I can't read it!"

During math especially,

2 and 3, 8 and 9
were impossible to tell apart,
and the confusion only grew.

We did look at the test questions—

at least, technically we did—
but there was no way to tell what we were looking at.
The quality of those test papers was so miserable
that most of the time the teacher ended up
rewriting every question on the blackboard
before we could even start the exam.

Under those conditions,

cheating wasn't even a concept.
There was nothing clear enough to cheat from.

One day, while I was playing with Minji—

my desk partner from the neighborhood—
I told her about helping print the test papers.
When she heard that we had another test the next day,
she panicked and insisted we come up with a countermeasure.
Thus began our grand conspiracy:
the test paper leak.


Plan 1:
Help with the mimeograph printing
and secretly memorize the questions.


Plan 2:
If the printing was already finished,
they must have thrown the scrap sheets away—
so we'd dig through the trash
and recover the test papers.



We marched to school full of grand ambition—
only to find that the mimeograph work was already finished,
and the trash cans had been cleaned out spotless.

Minji collapsed in despair.

"How am I supposed to take the test tomorrow?
I can't study at all..."

So I said, casually,

"I'll let you copy mine tomorrow."

Her eyes lit up instantly.
"If I do well on the test,
I'll give you all my marbles—every single one!
So you gotta show me properly, okay?"

The next day during class,

our homeroom teacher handed back the graded tests.

I got a hundred.

She got ninety.

I leaned over and whispered to Minji,

"You know you gotta give me all your marbles later, right?"
I said it with a straight face.

She stayed quiet until the very end of class.

Then, the moment recess—play time—started,
she bolted out of the classroom.

I ran after her,

but she kept sprinting
until she dove into the girls' restroom
and locked the door from the inside.

I picked up a small stone

and wedged it under the door from the outside
so it couldn't be pushed open.
Then I calmly went back to the classroom.


But Minji—who I thought would come out soon—

never returned, even after the next class began.

Suddenly, fear hit me.

All kinds of thoughts ran through my head,
and then one horrible idea flashed up:
What if she slipped and drowned in the toilet?

A chill ran through my whole body.

I told the teacher I needed to go to the bathroom,

then hurried back to the restroom
where I had wedged the stone under the door.

From inside,

I heard Minji crying.

Every time she pushed the door outward,

the stone stayed jammed tight
between the door and the floor,
refusing to budge.

"Minji, move away from the door!" I shouted,

then kicked it hard from the outside—bang, bang.

The stone popped loose and rolled away,

and Minji stumbled out,
her face a mess of tears and snot.

"Are you okay?" I asked.

She didn't answer.

She just kept crying
and walked straight back to the classroom.

After that, Minji never spoke to me again.

I was just relieved that Minji was safe.
After that, I made up my mind never to fool around in a bathroom again.


And on my elementary school report card,
there was always the same line written every year:


"Plays pranks excessively."

chapters.title: Scene 2 - Food Poisoning
chapters.content:
According to my mother, once my father made up his mind to close down the boarding house, there were all sorts of dealings back and forth for days. In the end, he handed the place over to one of his old friends.

Whenever my father was out of sight, I used to wander over to Jungho's house.

The moment you opened their door, you could smell the way that family lived. Beside the gate stood a strange bonsai—branches twisted like snakes climbing a tree. At the end of the wooden porch sat a tiny apple tree, bearing red fruits no bigger than a marble, shining brrrrightly, pretty as lacquer.

But if you plucked one and bit into it, your mouth went dry as dust and you'd spit it out.

"Tweh! Tweh-tweh!"

Then the adults behind you would burst out laughing.

"It's only pretty to look at, kid."

In the old guest room, Father and his friends used to kill time with mahjong or cards. They would stack mahjong tiles like a wall, rattle the dice, line up those thin white sticks, and play with loud thunk, thunk sounds.

I didn't know a single rule, but I'd crouch behind Father, watch that secret world of grown-ups, and eventually doze off right there.

One evening, Mother called Seonju-nuna in a hurry.

"Hey, come with me—quick."

And they left for Jungho's house.

Two hours later, Mother slammed the door as she came in and clicked her tongue.

"Aigo... people say raising sons is useless. Damn it! Idiots!"

I was digging my ear and asked,

"What happened?"

Seonju-nuna let out a long sigh.

"Jungho's mom got food poisoning. She threw up and had diarrhea... ruined all her clothes and blankets."

I snorted.

"That's nothing. Just wash it."

Nuna shook her head.

"That's not the problem. She stayed like that for two whole days because the men in the house didn't change her clothes."

My eyes grew round.

"What? Why not?"

"They were supposed to wash her, but they... couldn't bring themselves to pull down their own mother's underclothes. When she asked why, they said, 'How can we undress our mother down there?' and froze."

I let out a helpless laugh.

"Well... that house is full of men. That must've been rough."

But Nuna kept looking straight at me.

"Then tell me, if our mother ends up like that someday, what will you do?"

I scratched my head.

"Who knows? Probably all the aunties will come running. Chungju-aunt, Jeongchachon-sister-in-law..."

"What if nobody's around?"

Nuna's voice was serious.

I paused.

"You mean—just sons at home? Then our mother will handle it herself. She's got the temper of a tiger. Even twenty grown men together can't stop her."

Nuna giggled.

"True. Even smallpox and tiger ghosts would step aside for Mother."

I dug my ear again.

"I'll ask Father-in-law tomorrow. If you ever get food poisoning... I guess I'll be the one to clean it, right?"

Nuna's face suddenly flushed red. She bit her lip.

"We still didn't have any... honey~~~"

She tried to continue, but pinched her thigh to keep from laughing.

I pretended not to notice.

"What? Honey? Pot? Party? You speak English loud today? Then why are you pinching that poor little thigh?"

Nuna jumped back, flustered.

"I—I suddenly have stomachache!"

And she ran out of the room like she was escaping a crime scene.

Watching her flee, I scratched my nose and murmured,

"Life's got no answers... when even mothers and sons turn out like this."

chapters.title: Scene 3 - Letter from Odin's Kingdom 2
chapters.content:
Dearest! Mein Kaiser!

You once told me that a tree cannot simply be transplanted into foreign soil. Only now do I understand the full weight of that truth.

Here in Odin's Kingdom, ghosts live completely severed from their own realm.

No safety nets.
No redemption arcs.
No "next life."

Just taxes, survival, and the cold wind that polishes the bone.

But in your kingdom?

A ghost may sin, be punished, serve the sentence, and rise again—
not as ash, but as life.

Your welfare system... yes, it empties my pockets—
but at least it exists.

Here?

Only frost.

Humans distrust ghosts, ghosts distrust humans, and neither side bothers to listen to the other's heartbeat.

And yet—
I have made a friend.

Her name is Huldra.

We grew close sharing the kimchi and ramyeon you sent. She called the taste "heaven-warm"—a warmth she had never touched in life or in death.

If you ever open a gate in your kingdom, she wishes to follow me through it.

Sincerely,
your loyal trainee.


P.S.

"General, your kingdom is strange.
In your land, even ghosts are given a second life.
Here in Odin's world, we don't get 'second.'
We barely get 'first.'"

"In your land, a ghost who makes a mistake goes to prison, yes—
but afterward they are allowed to be reborn,
to work again,
to love again.
That is mercy.
That is welfare.
That is dignity."

"But here?
We pay our tax,
we starve alone,
we freeze alone,
and no human hears our voices.
Your kingdom feels... warmer than life itself."

"General, I finally understand what you meant:
Even the dead deserve a chance to live."

chapters.title: Scene 4 - Dandelion Pickle
chapters.content:
I was in second grade, so most of it has faded, but I still remember this much:

On the way down to the wash place, my mother set big and small stones into the mud, pressing them down with her bare hands to make steps for the women to walk safely.

That path led to a wide field—forty meters across, maybe two hundred meters long. Its edges were walled with earth and stone, a meter high, like a small fortress. Hard to reach unless you knew where to climb.

When winter loosened its grip, when the ice cracked and the willow buds fluffed out—the village women headed to that field with baskets on their heads and children dangling from their hands.

I wasn't supposed to run around like other kids. I took medicine every day, and my body was always a little slower, a little weaker. But the older girls never went without me.

They'd break off willow buds and press them into my palms.

Soft as rabbit fur.
Warm as a quilt straight from sunlight.

While the children chased each other in the grass, the women knelt with their hoes, digging up 'Naeng-i' and 'mugwort'. The older girls helped—cheeks flushed, sleeves rolled, like they were already small versions of the women they would someday become.

After an hour or two, when the baskets were half full of spring greens, the girls finally sat in a circle and began making dandelion jewelry.

Seon-ae-nuna—golden-handed Seon-ae—and Kongju-nuna braided crowns, rings, and necklaces. Their hair caught the spring light, and the crowns glowed like halos.

Of course I begged for one. So they made me a tiny crown too.

The dandelion stems—thin, bright, green with a hint of blue—looked fragile, but once woven, they held together like rope.

We wore our crowns, rings on our fingers, and chased each other across the field until the sky began to cool.

The next morning, our house filled with the smell of 'Naengi Doenjang Soup'—spring in a bowl.

The day after that, the women mixed mugwort into dough and made 'Sugbeomuri'—a kind of mugwort rice cake to share with every house.

But my mother—she saved the dandelion stems. She washed them clean, tied them in bundles, and placed them into an earthen jar.

Then she boiled soy sauce and poured it over them—'Dandelion Jang-a-jji'.

A month later, we ate it with dalrae namul.

Salty, bitter, sweet.
Like the taste of early spring.

But those spring days didn't last.

Maybe I was in fourth grade when the typhoon came. Rain hammered the ground for days. The adults couldn't sleep—worried the river would overflow.

We children peeked outside, just to see how high the water was rising. Even that was enough to be scolded.

"It's dangerous! Back inside—NOW!"

The water kept climbing, brown and heavy, like a beast waking up.

On TV they said pigs from farmhouses were being swept away. I stared at the river and felt something cold in my bones.

In the end, the river didn't flood the village—but it did take everything else.

The field where we ran.
The earthen wall like a fortress.
The small plots above it.

Gone.
All gone.

The ground looked as if a 'Gigantic Cat' had dragged its claws through it—a long, quiet wound left on the land.

Later, the county rebuilt the land with retaining walls and concrete channels. But the place where we laughed, the place where spring lived—that never came back.

That was the year I learned nature isn't "pretty." It's an emperor. It gives, and it takes, without apology.

chapters.title: Scene 5 - Bossam-jil (Widow-napping)
chapters.content:
There was one rule in our house that could never be broken.

"Save on anything you want—
but never on books."

So my mother bought the entire 500-volume set
of the Ministry of Education's Recommended Books for Youth
and lined one side of our living room wall
with a heavy, imposing bookshelf.

Every month she subscribed to Newton,
and never missed an issue of Sonyeon Joongang or Bomulseom.
The stories poured into our home
like mischievous children
who never knew how to behave.

I remember thinking,
There's no way I'll ever read all of this.

But that's how life works.
In the end,
I read almost all of it.

In Eunpunggol,
big and small troubles
always seemed to pass through our house first.

One summer,
a man from the village ran off
with a widow.
It was a clumsy kind of bossam-jil.

Her father was furious,
and the man had nothing—
no money,
no place to hide.

In the end,
he brought the widow
straight to our house,
threw himself down on the wooden porch,
and begged my mother to save them.

My mother seated the two of them on the porch.
She didn't raise her voice.
She didn't get angry.

After a long silence,
she spoke.

"Juguk," she said.
"This isn't something
that can be brushed aside."

Then she added,

"You may have to lose a finger."

At those words,
Juguk and Yeon-hui
said nothing.

That very night,
the two of them fled the village.

A few days later,
people said,

"If they don't even have that kind of nerve,
raising children would be impossible anyway."

And that was the end of it.

That night,
I told the story to Seonju.

She stayed silent for a long time.

I spoke quietly.

"Getting married,
having children—
those aren't things you start
without thinking."

After a brief pause,
I added,

"It's something you enter
with your life on the line."


Seonju smiled and asked,

"So... did you risk your life
to marry me too?"

I pointed to the bookshelf.

"Pick a book."

She pulled out Samgang Oryun
and So-nyeo-gyeong.

"I know this one," she said,
"but what on earth
is this shameless book?"

"That shameless book," I replied,
"was officially designated
as recommended reading for teenagers
by the Ministry of Education."

"For real?"

"Want me to call my mom?"

"No!
I'm just... trying to understand."

"I don't teach for free.
What are you going to give me?"

"What do I even have to give?"

"Then at least act cute.
My mother always said—
a man can live with a clever fox,
but never with a clueless bear."

After hesitating for a long moment,
Seonju twisted her body awkwardly and said,

"Honeyyy~~
my sweet honeyyy~~
this foolish maiden wishes to learn.
Won't you teach me~?"

That night,
I gave her a small lecture.

"Samgang Oryun
is a moral code from the Joseon era.
Even now, during holidays or ancestral rites,
you still hear elders quote it.

But modern scholars don't think
it fits our time anymore.
Sex education is necessary, of course,
but teaching it openly
always causes trouble.

So they slipped it quietly
into the list of recommended books,
hoping kids would figure things out on their own.

Maybe that was
the last bit of conscience
our intellectuals had left."

"Juguk's case was the same.
They had to be shamed in front of the village elders—
that was the only way
they could stand upright afterward.

Normally,
a man confesses his feelings,
the woman accepts,
they greet the elders,
and then the families exchange a proper proposal.

There's an order to these things.

If you skip all that
and jump straight to bossam?
That's not romance.
That's kidnapping.

Even back in the Joseon era,
there were unspoken ways
to tell whether two people
were truly in love."

Seonju stared at me.

"And how do you know all this,
my dear husband?"

"Read a 500-volume collection cover to cover
and live with my mother for ten years.
After that,
you just know things automatically."

She opened So-nyeo-gyeong,
her eyes narrowing.

"Then...
how do you do this part?"

"That," I said,
"requires a monthly tuition fee."

She pouted and spread out the blanket.

"This poor maiden
has no such fee..."

"I told you earlier—
a woman must be a fox,
not a bear."

Suddenly she jumped up and started dancing.

"You are the dancing queen~
young and sweet~~~~"

The rafters shook.
The brass pots in the kitchen rattled.
Even the jars in the yard
seemed to dance along.

That night,
Madam Chungju leaned toward my mother
and whispered,

"Those two...
they're going to break every honeypot
in this house tonight."

My mother didn't even blink.
She simply nodded and murmured,

"It's their season now... isn't it?"

chapters.title: Scene 6 - Guest from Odin's Kingdom
chapters.content:
Ms. M returned from Odin's Kingdom.
She bowed deeply before Yeomra, the King of Death,
and then came straight to me—
someone quiet, tall, and unfamiliar walking behind her.

Ms. M
"General! Please allow me to bow to you first!"

I laughed softly.
"Well, well... the King already told me everything."

Ms. M
"Thanks to you, I learned so much.
I experienced things I never imagined.
From now on, I will serve you with all my loyal heart."

Me
"Graduated cum laude, huh? I'm proud of you.
You're no longer just a ghost or a messenger—you know that, right?"


Ms. M
"Yes, sir! Ready for orders, sir!"

Me
"Easy. You need a proper rest.
With your family... and with your new husband.
But before that—I hear you brought me a guest."

Ms. M
"Yes, sir. This is Huldra, from Odin's Kingdom.
Huldra, please introduce yourself to my General."

Huldra bowed so gracefully it almost looked like a ritual.

Huldra
"General... I humbly present myself.
It is an honor to meet you.
My king—Odin—often spoke of you.
He said, 'Nothing in this world or the next can compare to him.'"

Me
"I used to visit Odin's Kingdom for chess.
He was one of my toughest opponents.
Huldra—from today on, you follow my rules.
Agent M, guide her to her new quarters."

Huldra
"Thank you, sir!"

I added, almost as an afterthought—

Me
"And... about that incident.
You have my thanks.
You saved a girl—Nadia Comăneci.

Some fool down here fell in love with her just from watching TV.

And worse—even a Dokkaebi became obsessed.
If you hadn't intervened,
we would've had chaos... on both sides."

Agent M
"...Sir, the Dokkaebi kept shouting,
'How can a human bend like that?! She must be one of us!!'
It took three officers to hold him down."

I groaned.

Me
"That creature always falls for the wrong women.
First Vanna White...
Then Nadia Comăneci...
What's next? Princess Diana?"

Huldra whispered, puzzled—

Huldra
"...What is a TV?"

Me
"You'll find one in your room.
Go see it yourself. But don't fall in love with anyone."

I waved my hand.

"Alright—meetingdismissed. Go home. Rest."

chapters.title: Scene 7 - Taste of Tobacco
chapters.content:
There was a small tobacco shop right next to our house.
Sirak lived there with his grandmother,
and I ran errands for them almost every day—
buying cigarettes with names that sounded like magic spells.

Hwanhee, Sol, 88, Hansando, Taeyang, Saemaeul, Rose...

My father usually smoked Hwanhee or Sol,
and my mother preferred 88.
Even now, I can't explain why that number—88—
looked so cool and confident on a cigarette pack.
Back then, those brand names felt like tiny passwords
to a world only adults were allowed to ente

Between Sirak's tobacco shop and the hardware store next door
ran a narrow alley—
just wide enough for kids to squeeze in sideways
and just secret enough to feel like our own kingdom.

That was where Sirak and the neighborhood boys gathered every day,
playing marbles, slapping down paper game cards,
spinning tops until the dirt floor trembled.

Sirak was always inventing a new game,
a new rule,
a new kind of mischief.

To us,
he wasn't just the oldest kid in the alley—
he was the undisputed boss of our little world.

One early winter day,
Sirak-hyung was hammering and scraping away at something—
ttuk-ttak, sseuk-sseuk-ssak-ssak—
so I went to see what he was up to.

It was a sled.

The other boys quickly copied him,
but I was clumsy and kept fumbling with the wood.
Sirak-hyung watched me struggle for a moment,
then built one for me in just a few strokes—
clean, swift, effortless.

Sirak's family also farmed tobacco.
In summer, they harvested the long, heavy leaves,
steamed them in a great curing barn,
dried them until they turned the color of old brass,
and sold them to the Korea Tobacco & Ginseng Corporation.


One afternoon after school,
I stopped by Sirak-hyung's place.
His family—and half the neighborhood kids—
were threading tobacco leaves onto long ropes,
one leaf after another,

like stringing beads of sunlight.

We thought it was the funniest thing,
so we giggled and helped,
our small hands clumsy but eager,
laughing at how the leaves brushed our faces
with their sweet, earthy smell.

Then one of the elders said,
"If you dry these right and smoke them in a 'Gom-bang-dae' pipe,
the flavor is unbelievable."

One kid piped up with a snort,
"But I heard the ones you buy at the store taste better than that!"

The elder clicked his tongue.
"Aish—what do you kids know about the taste of tobacco?"

"Maybe it tastes bad 'cause you messed it up.
Simple as that~."

The adults burst into loud laughter.
"Our Dong-gi really knows a thing or two!
Alright then—can you teach us how to make tobacco taste good?"

I nodded like a little master.
"Well, it depends on what each gentleman likes.
...some elders like it sweet—add a little sugar and a pinch of MSG, you know, that seasoning powder called Miwon."
And some of you like it sharp and cool—so you mix in peppermint or a touch of cinnamon."


The adults roared with laughter,
slapping their knees and wiping their eyes.

Then one mischievous elder leaned in and asked
"Well then, how do you make it... nutty?"

I suddenly realized,
"Ah... this is grown-ups teasing me."

So I thought of that nutty sesame-oil smell
that rises when you roll gimbap—
and a brilliant idea struck me:

"If you brush sesame oil on tobacco leaves
and then smoke them...
wouldn't they smell wonderfully nutty too?"

So I answered with complete seriousness.

"Oh, that one's a bit tricky," I replied gravely.
"First, you dry the leaves perfectly and press them flat.
Then you brush them—very gently—with sesame oil,
let them rest in the shade for a week,
sprinkle just a pinch of seasoned salt,
and finally grill them over charcoal...
front and back... just a little... just enough."

By this point, the adults were laughing so hard
they were wiping tears from their eyes.

"Our Dong-gi knows every tobacco flavor!"
one of them hollered.
"Look at him—he's the greatest elder in all of Eunpunggol!"

And before I knew what was happening,
they hoisted me up onto someone's shoulders,
parading me around the alley
like I'd just become the village chief.

Seeing all this, the other elders turned to my mother and said:

"Where on earth did you get a boy like that?"
"Unbelievable—absolutely unexplainable how sharp he is."
"That kid's silver tongue is the best in the whole village!"
"I swear, Eunpunggol might finally have a true prodigy."

My mother listened to their praise
with a quiet, satisfied smile.

That night, Seonju spoke up.
"Seobangnim-Honey... will you teach me how cigarettes taste?"

I snapped back, playing the stern husband,
"Hey now—kids shouldn't know such things."


She burst into laughter,
and the sound of it—light, careless, warm—
slipped out the window
and drifted into the alley where summer was ending.

And just like that,
between the fading heat of August
and the first chilly breath of autumn,
the two of us were tangled
in a season of sweet, ridiculous days.

chapters.title: Scene 8 - A man from GIA (Ghost Intelligence Agency)
chapters.content:
A man from GIA(Ghost Intelligence Agency)

A man from GIA visited today.
And it nearly killed Agent M.

That night,
Agent M exploded into my house—
hair electrified, eyes spinning,
like she had sprinted across seven hell realms.

"GENERAL! GENERAL! A man—
a man came to see us!!"

I calmly set down my tea.

"Agent M...
inhale.
Exhale.
Good.
Now—who came?"

She gulped and whispered as if naming a forbidden god:

"A man from... GIA."

I blinked.

"GIA?
What the hell are they doing here?"

Her jaw unhinged.

"Sir—you know GIA??"

I blinked again.

"Of course I know.
Ghost Intelligence Agency.
What else would GIA stand for?
'Ghosts In Aprons'?"

Agent M nearly dropped dead on the spot.

"SIR!!
How—how do you know that?!"

I rubbed my temples.

"I was the 46th CEO of it.
You didn't know?"

Her mouth opened like a drawer someone forgot to install stoppers on.

"Wh—wh—WOOOOW...!!!
Sir!!
What do we do?!
How do we respond to GIA?!"

I waved her off.

"Easy.
Tell them:
'The top secret!

Recipe of tobacco is sesame oil."

Agent M froze solid.

"S–sir...
you're... serious?"

I said

"Completely serious.
Go.
Say it.
Now."

Agent M saluted like she was facing Divine Judgment.

"Yes, sir!!!
RIGHT AWAY SIR!!"

And she blasted out of the house—
presumably to deliver the most impressive message
ever received by the Ghost Intelligence Agency
since its founding in the Paleolithic Era.

chapters.title: Scene 9 - Harvest
chapters.content:
Behind our house stood the Rubber Shoe Shop.
When I was growing up, it looked like an ordinary little shoe store—
but people said it had been selling rubber shoes since waaay back in the old days.

I used to wonder,
"So there really was a time when even black rubber shoes were precious..."

For me, life was simpler:
white rubber shoes for playing in the water,
and sneakers for everything else.

And as for the Rubber Shoe Shop...

The people who ran that rubber shoe shop
were probably from the same clan as my great-great-grandfather.
The uncle there held a higher rank in the family hierarchy—
one of the very few above me.

One autumn day, my mother said:

"Hey! Your uncle's threshing rice today.
Go help him!"

"Where?"

"Just keep walking past the church
toward Jeongcha Village.
You'll see your uncle there."

So I wondered how rice threshing was actually done...

I had seen bean threshing before—
dry the beans, spread a tarp in front of the house,
and beat them with a 'Dorikkae'.

But rice?

I had only watched from afar...
never tried it myself.

As I walked toward Jeongja Village,
I saw a group of people gathered.

"Dong-gi! Come over here~~!"

"Yes, uncle! What should I do?"

"When the folks run the thresher,
the rice grains come out on one side
and the straw comes out on the other."

"You take the straw bundles
and stack them over there by the cultivator."

It was my first time, so everything felt fun.

Since it was already past noon,
the aunti and village ladies arrived
carrying a big washbasin filled with lunch

.

"Dong-gi! Come eat!"

They mixed it all together for me—
barley rice with a spoonful of 'Doenjang',
fresh lettuce seasoned with chili flakes,
a ladle of soybean paste soup,
a handful of raw radish slices,
a fried egg laid gently on top,
one spoon of sesame oil,
and a big, heaping scoop of 'Kko-i-jang'—
our thick, rustic red pepper source.

They mixed it with both hands,
as if making a blessing instead of a meal.

The Auntie asked me,

"Is it good?"

"Yes! It's really good, ma'am."

She laughed.
"Your family eats meat every day, don't they?"

"Meat never tastes like this."

"Really now? Already finished?
Should I give you another bowl?"

"Wow!, Auntie, I'm full to death.
Please... just give me some 'Sikhye'-sweet rice-boiled soup."

"Alright, here you go."

She poured 'Sikhye' into my rice bowl—
and I swear,
I had never tasted anything so sweet.

"Tired yet?"

"Not really, ma'am.
If I keep going a little more,

we'll be done soon anyway."

"Alright then.

Later, ride back on the cultivator."

I was just a kid—
how much help could I really be?
But I never complained,
never made a sour face,
and because of that,
everyone there treated me with such warmth...
as if I were the village's own little son.

The rice fields had turned golden,

their soft under-skin showing through so dark
it was almost black.

When the sun began to sink
beyond the mountain ridge,
the elders called out to me:

"Dong-gi! Come here!"

"Yes!" I shouted,

running toward them.

One of them lifted me up
and set me gently
on top of the bundles of rice straw
loaded on the cultivator.

And with the engine rattling
'tur-tur-tur,'
I fell asleep—
a small child rocked by the sound—
as the day,
quietly and beautifully,
came to its end.

chapters.title: Scene 10 - The Smell of Ramyeon 2
chapters.content:
One day, Messenger and Agent M burst into my house—
faces red, hair exploding, breathing like they had outrun a thunderstorm.

Messenger: "Sir!! I have... a report!!"
Me: "...What now."
Messenger: "Huldra... got pregnant!!!"
Me: "Good. And?"
Agent M: "That is all sir!."

I put my cup down.

Me:
"Messenger, prepare a live broadcast through GBS—Ghost Broadcasting System.
In one hour. Let Odin and Yeomra know.
Agent M, bring the GIA guy to witness my judgment.
And summon Huldra and the Dokkaebi.
Now."

The couple:
"Y-yes, sir!!!"

One Hour Later — The Trial Begins

Huldra and the Dokkaebi knelt before me like two soaked puppies.

Me:
"First of all—
Odin and King Yeomra are watching this.
Live.
On TV.
All ghosts from both realms too.
Isn't that fantastic?"

The couple:
"...Sir... it's a bit too much..."

Me:
"Too much?
You broke my TV.
And my rules.
That's a straight ticket to the Fire-Burning Abyss!
Huldra—tell me.
Who is the father?"

Huldra: "...The Dokkaebi... sir."

Me:
"Dokkaebi!
Why did she designate you as the father?"

Dokkaebi:
"I-I don't know, sir...
But maybe... I have one clue.
I... watched TV... in her room sometimes..."

Me:
"Strange.
I gave EACH of you your OWN television.
Why were you watching in her room?"

Dokkaebi:
"I only taught her how to cook ramyeon!
And we shared kimchi... sir..."

Me:
"Huldra? Is that true?"

Huldra:
"Yes, sir... completely true."

Me:
"Ramyeon and kimchi...
Humanism?
No—Ghostism!"

Huldra: "Sir... it was delicious..."
Dokkaebi: "Best ramyeon in nine realms, sir..."

Me: "And soju??"

Huldra:
"...Drinking alone is lonely...
So I... asked him to join..."

Me:
"...Fair.
Soju does require another soul."

At that time, Yeomra and Odin thought of her as a troublemaker.

Ramyeon Cross‑Examination

Me:
"Now answer—ON THREE.
'Ramyeon and kimchi are delicious and yummy.'
Three!"

The couple:
"Yes, sir!! Delicious and yummy!!"

Me:
"Good.
Ramyeon and kimchi—is that Humanism?
Three!"

The couple:
"Of course, sir!"

Me:
"Ramyeon + kimchi + soju = friendship?"

The couple:
"Absolutely, sir!"

Me:
"Very good.
A man and a woman cannot be 'just friends.'
Three."

The couple:
"No doubt, sir!!"

Me:
"And if it's deeper than friendship...
that's love."

The couple:
"Right, sir!"

Me:
"And love... can make a baby.
Three... two..."

The couple (surrendered):
"Right, sir......"

THE FINAL VERDICT

Me:
"When in Rome, do as Romans do.
When in Korea—
you marry,
raise your kids,
and serve kimchi properly.
Three! Two! One!"

The couple:
"!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!"

Me:
"Odin and Yeomra just called.
Both kings bless your marriage.
Agent M—prepare their honeymoon suite.
...and bring some ginseng for her.
Huldra needs strength—
love burns a lot of energy."

Agent M:
"Yes, sir. Premium grade.
Six-year root.
Steamed twice."

Dokkaebi (timidly raising a hand):
"Sir... can I have one too...?"

Me:
"No.
You already used your strength."

I waved my hand toward the darkness—
toward Odin's realm, toward the underworld,
toward every ghost watching on GBS.

"Live well.
And,,,,,

Do not mess up!

Done."

chapters.title: Scene 1 - Head of the Household
chapters.content:
One summer—or maybe autumn—after the market had ended,
in that hour when the day's dust settles with the sunlight,
the village elders carried our house's wooden porch
and set it down in front of Dongnyeon's house.

As always, a janggi board was laid out on one side,
and the women sat together on the other, talking.

No one remembered how it started,
but the women soon went inside
and came back out with a frying pan, flour, a ladle, cooking oil,
garlic chives, green onions, and a portable gas range.

They mixed the white flour with water into a thick batter.

The pan went on the flame.
Oil shimmered, then bubbled.

A ladleful poured in—

chiiiiii—

An unnamed pancake began to cook.

I was playing janggi with the adults
when a girl from my class, Yongju, said he wanted some jelly.

I suddenly felt like teasing him.

"Yongju! I'll give you some. Hold out your hand."

She did.

"If it's something precious,
you should receive it properly—with both hands."

So She brought both hands together.

"You didn't wash them, did you?
Then it won't taste good. Open your mouth instead."

The fool stepped closer.

"Aaaaaah—"

I dropped something black and soft into her mouth.

She chewed.

Then—

"Hey, you jerk! Isn't this a booger?!"

And She burst into tears.

The adults, who had been watching from the side, burst out laughing.

I said,

"Do you usually eat boogers?
How else would you know so fast?"

Yongju's father laughed the loudest.

"Dong-gi's right!
Looks like our Yongju eats them all the time!"

Yongju, embarrassed, stopped crying soon enough.

Her father suddenly lifted me onto her shoulders
and walked around the neighborhood, shouting,

"Dong-gi is this village's treasure!
When the grown-ups get bored,
he's the one who makes things interesting!"

That felt strange.

Usually, my mother—or someone—would've scolded me.

But that day, everyone only smiled.

He set me down.

"Dong-gi.
You should keep getting along with Yongju."

He held out her little finger.

I hooked mine around it
and sealed the promise.

A few months later,
I heard that Yongju's father had died of cancer.

After that, their family gave up the business.
The door of "Yongju-Kokne Hair Salon" never opened again.

The alley between their house and Dongnyeon's—
the one we used to take to Pine Tree Garden—
was blocked by a large gate.

The wall grew higher.

After that,
whenever I saw Yongju,
that moment came back to me.

So I never spoke to her again.
Never teased her.

Until I graduated middle school
and left for Seoul,

I don't remember
ever having another conversation with her.

At the market, around that time,
several households lost their fathers.

Their doors closed.

They became cut off from the village.

It was then, vaguely,
that I began to understand—

when the head of a household dies,
life becomes harder.

And in Eunpunggol,
his absence
meant poverty.

chapters.title: Scene 2 - Once Upon a Time on the Radio
chapters.content:
DJ:

Alright—
our next letter.

Before I begin,
I should say this.

The producers were laughing...
and then suddenly very quiet.

It's a Lunar New Year story.

From Northern Europe.

The sender—

Huldra.

LETTER

Hello.

My name is Huldra.
I come from the far North—
from Odin's lands.

When I first came to Korea,
I thought winter would be easier.

It's farther south, after all.

DJ:

That assumption...
never ends well.

LETTER

In my homeland,
temperatures fall much lower.

But Korea—

is different.

Minus fifteen degrees,
and the moment you step outside—

the wind hits you
like a knife.

For a second,
you forget how to breathe.

DJ:

In Korea,
winter isn't about numbers.

It's about the wind.

LETTER

That winter,
I survived by washing
only my hands and face.

Then one day—

Ms. M said,

"No matter how cold it is,
you must welcome the New Year clean."

"Let's go to the bathhouse."

DJ:

That's not a suggestion.

That's a command.

LETTER

At the bathhouse—

even ghosts were there.

Men over fifteen
weren't allowed inside.

So we left her son outside
and went in.

People didn't just wash and leave.

They soaked.

Ten minutes.
Twenty.

Then sat down—

and scrubbed
their skin

with towels
like sandpaper.

Ms. M finished first.

Then she turned—
toward me.

DJ:

Uh-oh.

LETTER

She started scrubbing me.

I said it hurt.

I told her to stop.

She didn't.

Then I saw it.

Dark flakes
rolling off my skin.

Falling everywhere.

I felt ashamed.

Was I really this dirty?

But the other women—

even the ghosts—

smiled.

"We all live like that."

"Nothing to be embarrassed about."

DJ (quietly):

...that line stays.

LETTER

Then—

it happened.

Ms. M was showering.

Suddenly—

BOOM.

The wall collapsed.

Completely.

Everyone froze.

Then screamed.

We grabbed towels
and ran—

like dodging a bomb.

DJ:

Wait...
this is a New Year story??

LETTER

They covered the hole
with a tarp.

We got dressed.

Then we heard what happened.

Her son—

outside—

had tried to peek.

Knocked over fertilizer.

The sack hit the wall.

The wall gave way.

Her husband came running.

Apologized.

Paid for everything.

The women laughed.

"Kids will be kids."

And that was it.

DJ:

Up to here...
it's funny.

LETTER

At home,

the father scolded the boy.

Too ashamed
to face the neighborhood.

Ms. M said nothing.

Because—

when the wall collapsed—

she had hit her head.

And still,
she walked around calmly
for days.

DJ:

Wait.

The victim is the mother??

LETTER

Since coming to Korea—

this was the strangest
Lunar New Year
of my life.

But I still remember—

the warmth after,

clean skin,

and banana milk.

I hope
she recovered well.

And someday—

I hope we return
to that bathhouse together.

Thank you.

DJ (closing):

It starts funny.

...and honestly—

it stays funny.

Back then,
most houses didn't even have showers.

So on New Year's,
everyone went to the public bathhouse.

And things like this?

They happened
more often than you'd think.

Thank you, Huldra.

We'll send you a small gift.

Now—
let's listen to a song.

After Listening to the Radio

The story stayed light.

So—

I could joke about it too.

I called Agent M.


"Dokkaebi—
what is he doing these days?"

"He's learning to cook."

"Preparing for MCGW."

"Good."

"The turtle fleets need chefs."

"He's preparing
for his children."

"He's changed a lot."

"He's going to be a father."

"Excellent."

"There are ghosts
in Odin's kingdom
who want to come here."

"Set conditions."

"First—"

"They must be able
to get along
with Korean ghosts
and humans."

"Communication comes first."

"Yes, sir."

"Good."

"Time's up."

"Bye."

I watched her leave.

"Hey—
your boy
is still just a boy."

"Yes, sir."

She ran off
like the wind.

chapters.title: Scene 3 - Two Faces of the Wash-Place
chapters.content:
About thirty meters
from the wash-place,

there was a place
where water was held back.

A sluice gate.

Like a small dam.

People called it—

Cheondangbo.

During farming season,

when water ran short,

it mattered.

Water was drawn from there
into the fields.

It was a little over
two meters deep.

Kids who could swim well
played there sometimes.

One hot summer day—

on the way home
from school—

suddenly,

Byeongha's father
stepped into the water.

He was searching
for something.

And then—

a girl

none of us had ever seen

was pulled out.

We thought—

someone must have fallen in.

Someone pulled her out.

And we went home.

By evening,

we went back
to the riverside.

People were gathered.

Murmuring.

There was something—

covered
with straw bundles
and rice sacks.

The adults sat around it.

No one spoke.

When children tried to look—

someone shouted.

No one in particular.

"Hey!
Get back!"

"This is no place
for children."

The next day at school—

they said someone had drowned.

Teachers spoke all day
about water safety.

"Warm up first."

"Don't jump in."

"Don't go deeper
than your knees."

I just thought—

another accident.

A few days later—

a man came,

carrying bundles
of eggs.

Seonju and I
couldn't even hold them.

So we just stood there—

watching.

"Ma'am... thank you.
Truly... thank you."

"If it hadn't been for you—
we wouldn't have even seen
our youngest one
one last time."

"You're the one
who should be resting."

"And yet you came."

"We kept everyone away.
No one was allowed near."

"But when you shouted—
they moved."

"You said—"

'Shouldn't a father
at least see his daughter's face
on her final journey?'

"And you opened it."

"That's how—
we held her
one last time."

"I will never forget this."

Mother looked at him.

"Kindness?"

"Isn't that
just a parent's heart?"

"How could you not
see your youngest daughter—
one last time?"

"A child
you would have protected
even with your eyes."

"Go now."

"Steady yourself."

"After the harvest—
come again."

"...Yes."

The man fell to his knees.

He bowed.

Deeply.

Then—

he broke down again.

Mother placed a hand
on his shoulder.

Softly—

chanting.

Only then—

my mother,

and Byeongha's father—

began to look like

truly great people.

People to follow.

In that moment—

my mother

became someone

I could not reach.

Not even imagine reaching.

This is a story

I've never found easy

to speak aloud.

chapters.title: Scene 4 - Madam Kitchen (Bueokdaegi)
chapters.content:
Across the road
from my house,

there was a motorcycle shop.

It didn't sell many bikes.

Mostly—

repairs.

It was run
by a young man
in his early twenties.

Jinsung hyung.

One day—

I woke up from a nap.

The house felt...

busy.

Restless.

So I asked Seonju.

"Did something happen?"

"Someone came last night."

"Who?"

"Not family..."

"I don't know."


That evening,

my parents were talking
in low voices.

"Let her stay
for a few days."

"...Alright."

I asked what was going on.

My mother waited
until my father left.

Then—

she spoke.

"I was shocked."

"A grown woman
ran in—"

"completely naked."

"I couldn't
tell her to leave."


What Happened

Jinsung hyung
had been spending time

with youths
from nearby villages.

There was a girl
who liked him.

She said
she would marry him.

Her family said—

"Then you are no longer
our daughter."

"If you leave—
take nothing."

They meant it.

She left
with nothing.

Not even
underwear.

She went
to his house.

But—

it was locked.

He was away.

So she ran—

into our house.

My father said,

"Young men..."

"How do you stop blood
that's already boiling?"

Two days later—

they left together.

Started a life
of their own.

After

I said to Seonju,

"She's braver than you."

"I'm brave too."

"Would you have come
to me like that?"

"...Maybe."

"You know what I'd do
if you went to another man."

"I know."

"You've learned
some bad things."

"Then whose wife
am I?"

"...Alright."

"I lose."

She smiled.

Satisfied.

Madam Kitchen

"Bueokdaegi."

That was the name
of the second child
in that household.

After giving birth
to her first—

she became pregnant again
within a month.

When the time came,

she was resting
at home.

Then suddenly—

something felt wrong.

She sat down—

in the kitchen—

on a chamber pot.

And the baby—

came out.

Just like that.

My mother went over.

Cut the cord.

Helped deliver the child.

After that—

people called the baby,

"Bueokdaegi."

The kitchen child.

In those days,

women weren't always
called by their names.

They were called
by places.

By roles.

By where they came from.

I realized then—

why men
were drawn

to women
with wide hips
and full breasts.

It wasn't just desire.

It was instinct.

Recognizing someone—

who could carry life.

Who could hold
a household together.

After

Mother and Seonju
often looked after the baby.

They would smile—

and call her,

"Bueokdaegi."

chapters.title: Scene 5 - Two, Two, Two Babies
chapters.content:
I heard about Huldra's birth
in my office.

Suddenly—

BANG!

Agent M
and the Messenger

burst in
like the place was on fire.

"Sir! Big trouble!"

I didn't look up.

"Why is it always
big trouble?"

"What is it
this time?"

The Messenger
raised two fingers.

"Two—"

"Two people?"

He shook his head.

"Two—"

"Twelve?"

I laughed.

"Come on.
That's not even a meeting."

Agent M leaned in.

"Two—"

"Twenty?"

I waved my hand.

"Relax.
We'll manage."

I was already
back to my paperwork—

when suddenly—

"NO!!"

"Two."

...

"Hundred."

I froze.

Slowly—

very slowly—

I put my pen down.

"...Oh."

Dead silence.

I leaned back.

"That's not a problem."

A beat.

"That's a budget crisis."

Agent M swallowed.

I rubbed my forehead.

"Well then."

"Looks like
the Dokkaebi..."

"...needs to start
making real money."

A beat.

Then—

we all burst out laughing.

"Was the red ginseng buff
a bit too strong?"

No emergency meeting.

No action plan.

Just laughter—

echoing
through the office.

That day,

we officially decided—

not to count the children,

not to panic
about the forest,

and definitely—

not to touch
the red ginseng again.

At least—

for a while.

chapters.title: Scene 6 - Canvas Theater
chapters.content:
Every year,
in late summer—

Sirak hyung
and the neighborhood kids

started moving together.

I wondered
what they were doing.

They were selling
"invitations."

I don't remember the price—

but it was expensive
for a child.

If you passed
Hari Church,

there was a bridge
toward Georogi.

Under the bridge—

the stream
had dried up.

Only dirt.

Weeds.

They built it there.

A tent.

A projector.

They called it—

a cinema.

Near the entrance,

old movie posters
were taped up.

Layer
on top of layer.

"I heard this one's good."

People said that,

waiting
for the opening day.

The tent was made
of black cloth.

Two—
three layers thick.

No light
could get in.

Kids circled around,

looking—

for a way in.

A hole.

A gap.

Anything.

I didn't care much
about things like that.

But Jia nuna—

my older sister—

went.

With her friends.

She saw a few films.

The next day,

she wanted to go again.

She asked our mother
for money.

The answer—

no.

Then—

she used
the magic word.

"Dong-gi
has never seen a movie."

"He wants to go too."

"He's just not going
because it's dangerous."

"If I take him
with Seonae—"

"We'll just go
and come back."

"It's not for me."

"It's for him."

Mother knew.

Still—

she said,

"Alright."

"If it's the three of you—
this should be enough."

"Seonae—
watch him carefully."

Money changed hands.

I was taken—

like a hostage.


Still—

they found a good spot.

A flat stone.

They sat me down—

and started watching.

That day's film—

Taegkwon-V.

A turtle ship—

flying
through space.

By the time it started,

people had gathered.

From other neighborhoods.

A couple—

leaning
against each other.

The smell—

snacks from home.

Warm.

My mouth watered.

Sometimes—

the film snapped.

Stopped.

People murmured.

The owner ran—

changing reels.

Then—

it started again.

That's how we watched it.

The movie.

The people.

The moment.

And went home—

carrying
memories.

Someday—

I thought—

I should go
to Europe too.

chapters.title: Scene 7 - Manners Maketh a Woman
chapters.content:
When I stepped inside—

Seonju
was already sulking.

Her lips—

stretched out
in a full pout.

"So it's more fun
without me?"

"I'm worse than
an empty barley sack—
just lying there."

"You call yourself my husband,
and you go off alone
to watch something fun?"

"I'll go tomorrow."

"Alone."

She stuck out her tongue.

"Meh—roooong."

A grown woman—

like a child.

I just stood there.

So this—

this was
what people meant by

"bagaji."

Nagging
without sense.

Just then—

Mother's voice.

"Hey—
come out here. Now."

Seonju froze.

Then ran.

"I sent you
with your sister-in-law—"

"to build some bond."

"And this is
how you treat your husband?"

"Did he tell you to go first?"

"Did he say
he wanted to watch it?"

"People say you're pretty—"

"and now you think
you can't do wrong?"

When Mother started—

she didn't stop.

No one stepped in.

I nudged Seonju.

"Hurry—
say you're sorry."

Only then—

"Mother...
I was wrong."

"I didn't think
of your intention."

"I didn't think
of my husband."

"I was wrong."

Mother threw
the basket of corn—

onto the floor.

And went inside.

Seonju stood there.

Then—

quietly—

she picked up
each ear of corn.

Brushed off the dirt.

Placed them back.

One by one.

She went inside.

"Mother...
I was truly wrong."

"We'll eat this
gratefully."

Two days later—

Mother called her again.

"In this house—"

"whether man or woman—"

"the one who carries responsibility..."

"no matter how wrong they are—"

"...is not spoken to carelessly."

"That's our way."

"If someone isn't treated properly at home—"

"they'll be looked down on outside."

"And then—
who feeds this family?"

"Think about that first."

She handed over—

two videotapes.

"They said
these are worth watching."

That evening—

after dinner—

we watched.

The first film—

My Fair Lady.

Seonju watched—

quiet at first.

Then—

her eyes changed.

"Husband—"

"Did you watch
movies like this often?"

"Sometimes."

"In Seoul."

"Places like
Dansungsa."

"Daehan Theater."

"Really?"

"Then which was best?"

"This one."

"And Audrey Hepburn."

"She's the most beautiful woman
in the world."

Seonju blinked.

"Then why don't you live
with Audrey Hepburn?"

"Why me?"

I laughed.

"She's beautiful
on screen."

"But—"

"who could compare
to the woman sitting next to me?"

"Come on—
let me see your face again."

She turned away.

"Tch."

"So you do know
what pretty is."

I slid in
the second tape.

The Bourne Identity.

Gunfire.

Movement.

A man—

who didn't know
who he was.

But still—

he moved.

Like he knew.

Seonju whispered—

"Wow..."

I said nothing.

That night—

something changed.


Epilogue — Seonju's Diary

Today—

many strange things happened.

When I heard
he went without me—

something rose.

So I spoke.

Then—

Mother called.

And I knew.

"I was wrong."

That evening—

two tapes.

And one sentence—

"Manners
Maketh
a Woman."

The first film—

a woman learning—

how to speak,

how to stand,

how to become.

Watching her—

I saw

how small
my world had been.

The kitchen.

The yard.

That was all.

The second film—

a man moving—

without knowing who he was.

Still—

forward.

My husband—

was watching something else.

Not the scene.

The direction.

That look—

felt like

a path.

From that day—

I decided—

I would not remain
in the kitchen
and the yard.

I would see more.

Learn more.

Become more.

Even now—

I can still hear it—

softly—

"Lovely..."

chapters.title: Scene 8 - Autumn Sports Day
chapters.content:
When autumn came—

around September—

the boys practiced
chajeon-nori.

Wooden carts.
Pushing. Colliding.

Mock cavalry games.

The girls—

fan dances,

sogo drums,

running races,

tug-of-war,

ojaemi tossing.

At that age—

moving

was more fun
than studying.

Everything felt
like play.

On the morning
of Sports Day—

flags lined the field.

International flags—

fluttering
in the wind.

A tent—

for the principal,

teachers,

parents,

mothers.

Near the gate—

vendors.

Toys.

Snacks.

Things
we had never seen.

We couldn't look away.

The principal spoke.

Then—

each grade marched.

The band followed.

Pride.

Then the games—

ojaemi,

rolling balls.

The fan dance.

The drum dance.

Parents watched—

quietly.

Something
filling their chests.

Up to that point—

everything
was gentle.

Then—

chajeon-nori.

Heavy.

The boys underneath—

"It's heavy...
heavy..."

Still—

they pushed.

Blue team.

White team.

Manki.

Seok-hyung.

Gigap.

Names—

shouted
into the field.


In the afternoon—

races.

Sprints.

Relays.

We didn't care much
about ours.

We had seen them
too many times.

But—

the adults' games—

were different.

Tug-of-war.

Not a game.

A battlefield.

"Heave—ho!"

"Left—right!"

Bodies moving
as one.


Forearms—

tight.

Strained.

I couldn't
look away.

The mixed relay—

was everything.

Adults and students—

together.

A father.

A mother.

A brother.

A sister.

Passing the baton.

Running—

like something
was chasing them.

"Wooooah—!"

The field roared.

If the baton dropped—

a gasp.

If they caught up—

no one breathed.

By the end—

blue stamps
on our arms.

Notebooks.

Pencils.

Rewards.

Nearby—

makgeolli.

Shaken.

Poured.

Then—

as if waiting—

drums.

Jing.

Kkwaenggwari.

"Jing~~~~"

"Kkae-gaeng kkae-gaeng—"

Bodies moved.

I loved that.

It became a feast.

Watching the adults—

I realized—

they had been
holding it in.

All that time.

Work.

Labor.

Responsibility.

And today—

they let it out.

Someday—

we would be
like them.

Building lives.

And missing this.

But—

something felt off.

During military rule—

events like this
were used.

During colonial times—

games were used.

Control.

And yet—

people still laughed.

Still ran.

Still moved
together.

Maybe—

that was what
kept this place alive.

My mother—

head of
the parents' association.

Six years.

Preparing snacks.

Drinks.

Handling money.

Always—

at the beginning.

At the end.

Busy.

That's when
I learned—

whenever people gather—

someone

must do the work
no one sees.

Like oil—

keeping everything
moving.

That night—

my mother
and my wife—

sat together.

Counting.

Writing.

They didn't look at me.

Not once.

And I—

liked watching
my wife

change.

Little by little.

chapters.title: Scene 9 - Forbidden Love
chapters.content:
After Autumn Sports Day,

the ghosts

started acting strange.

Smiling more.

Softer voices.

Almost—

modern.

***** Text below is optional.*****



Something felt wrong.

So I called Agent M.

"What's going on
in the ghost community?"

"Love is in the air, sir."

"...What?"

"They had Sports Day."

"Since when
do ghosts have Sports Day?"

"Tug-of-war—
eye contact."

"Relay races—
hands brushing."

"Makgeolli—
shared from the same bowl."

A pause.

"Kissing happened."

I sighed.

BANG!

The Messenger burst in.

"Sir!
Serious situation!"

"It's always serious.
What now?"

"The Grim Reaper
has stopped working."

"...Stopped?"

"He fell in love."

"...With?"

"A water ghost."

"They met
during Sports Day."

Silence.

"King Yeomra
ordered immediate arrest."

I leaned back.

"Hold on."

"They can't be together anyway."

"Why not?"

"Why not?"

"The Grim Reaper
is a prosecutor."

"The water ghost—
an illegal resident."

"He's supposed
to arrest her."

The Messenger froze.

"...!!!"

Agent M spoke.

"They're in love, sir."

"Isn't there
another way?"

I thought.

"Isn't the underworld
overloaded these days?"

"Yes!"

"Overnight shifts—
every day!"

I nodded.

"Good."

"Tell her
to turn herself in."

"...Voluntarily?"

"Of course."

"Voluntary surrender—
reduced sentence."

The Messenger lit up.

"Assign her
to assist him."

"Rehabilitation
through labor."

"And after?"

I checked my notes.

"A hundred years."

A pause.

"After a hundred years
working together—"

"they'll be bonded."

"She learns the system."

"Like a private
becoming NCO."

Another beat.

"She becomes
a Grim Reaper."

"Then—"

"they can marry."

"Legally."

Silence.

"She's coming anyway."

"Better to surrender early."

"Lighter sentence."

"Stay in love."

Agent M stood.

"I think
I'll leave early today."

"Where?"

"To deliver
the good news."

I smiled.

"Love is powerful."

"Sometimes—"

"it's the only thing
that dissolves..."

"han."

I paused.

"We may see—"

"a sharp rise
in voluntary confessions."

Epilogue

After that—

voluntary surrenders
increased.

Dramatically.

The workload
stabilized.

Romance—

turned out to be
very effective policy.

chapters.title: Scene 10 - Song of Winter
chapters.content:
About fifty meters upstream
from the wash place—

Cheondangbo.

A small weir.

In summer—
it held water.

In winter—

it became ice.

Wide.

Long.

In the morning—

the sound came first.

jjajak—

jjajajak—

kunk.

It echoed
through the valley.

Along the bank—

dark earth.

Wet.

Only roots remained.

Dry stems—

from last autumn.

One morning—

after breakfast—

I picked up my sled.

And went.

"Dong-gi!"

Jinsung hyung.

From across the road.

I stopped.

He looked
at my sled.

"Hey—
lend me that runner."

He pulled it apart.

The iron spikes—

out.

A thick nail—

driven in.

Hammered.

Then—

ground.

Sharper.

Into the fire—

until it glowed.

Then—

into the snow.

chiiii—

Steam rose.

Steel hardened.

I watched.

And thought—

maybe—

he remembered.

On the ice—

I pushed.

Something was different.

Lighter.

Cleaner.

Each bite—

click.

click.

I moved forward.

Faster.


My wife—

gliding.

Then—

the wind.

Sudden.

Ice dust—

rose.

Hit us
like sand.

Everyone turned.

Waited.

Sometimes—

if you looked down—

you could see

fish.

Moving slowly.

And one leaf—

red.

From last autumn.

Drifting.

That's how we knew.

It was over.

Epilogue

A year later—

before they left
for the city—

Jinsung hyung's family
invited us.

We went.

Together.

Hobbang—

steamed.

Sweet potatoes—

roasted.

Quiet days.

Madam Kitchen—

sitting
with her family.


That—

is what I remember.

chapters.title: Scene 1 - Hobbang Time
chapters.content:
One winter day,
I invited the Dokkaebi, Huldra, the Messenger, Agent M,
and the Grim Reaper over.

I set a steamer on the stove,
steamed some Hobbang buns,
and we shared them—
chatting idly, without purpose.


I asked the Grim Reaper
how the water ghost had been doing.


I checked with Agent M
to see whether the head injury from last time
had fully healed.


Huldra said she gives birth to children
the way tree branches sprout from her back,
and that she had given birth to two hundred of them—
which finally satisfied everyone's curiosity
about how extraordinarily fertile she was.


Then the Dokkaebi suddenly
started rummaging through the bag of hobbang.


I asked what he was doing.


He said,
"I like vegetable hobbang~~"


I kicked him in the backside
and chased him outside.


"How can a Dokkaebi become a father
and still not grow up?"


Everyone burst out laughing.


And just like that,
we kept sharing hobbang
and talking late into the night.

chapters.title: Scene 2 - Branching Out (Bunga)
chapters.content:
At some point,
my mother began talking about building a new house.

"Honey," she said,
"I think it's time
the boys start living separately.
We could stack a few bricks
in the back yard behind the storage shed,
set up an oil boiler,
and use a motor pump."

My father replied,
half-heartedly,

"Why?
Why not let them endure married life a bit longer?
You always say
a child is still under our wing,
that you don't want to let Dong-gi go."

My mother answered,

"Even so,
it would be a waste to put Dong-gi into trade, wouldn't it?
You know it yourself—
in a house where people are constantly coming and going,
a man never turns out quite right.
He needs his own study.
Only then
does a person learn to think deeply."

Construction on the new house began,
and as I went back and forth to school,
I watched the site grow day by day.

I thought to myself,

"So this is it.
At last, a place where I can settle down.
A place where I won't have to live
listening to the sound of haggling."

But before the house was even finished,
my father said he had sold it.

I confronted him.

"Father!
You said it was going to be my house—
how can you sell it to someone else?
Isn't this the same as saying
we might as well cut ties as father and son?"


My mother snapped back in anger.

"Is there anything you can't say to your father?
Did you carry even a single brick?
Did you spread a bit of cement?
It's your father's house.
If he sells it, he sells it—
who are you to interfere?"

I had no argument left.
I was beaten by logic.

There was nothing more to say.

I accepted defeat,
turned away without a word,
and went into my room.

My wife was waiting for me there.

I said,

"Maybe... it just wasn't meant to be ours."

She tried to comfort me.

"It's just a house.
We can build another one later, can't we?
Let's wait a little longer."

I answered,

"A house can always be rebuilt.
That's not the problem."

She looked at me,
clearly not understanding
what I meant.

I said,

"People say fathers and sons are eternal enemies—
and that's how it is in our family.
This is just the beginning.
You'd better steel your heart too."

She laughed it off.

"Enemies?
A father and his son?
You're really saying all kinds of strange things today."

I replied,

"A mother is someone
who makes endless sacrifices
for the life born from her own body.
But a father—
a father gives everything
to the one he believes is the best.
That's why the bond between father and son
is so frightening."

I already knew it then.

No matter how much Eunpunggol was my hometown,
I would someday have to leave it.

The bitterness stayed with me—
the feeling that the house I might return to someday,
my very roots,
had already been pulled out of the ground.

Epilogue


Around that same time,
the fathers of my friends began passing away.
Some households slipped into poverty
almost overnight.


And one by one,
the young men
started leaving for the cities.

chapters.title: Scene 3 - Friends (After Hobbang Time)
chapters.content:
After Hobbang Time ended,
we all went our separate ways.

On their way home,
Grim and the Messenger stopped by the Dokkaebi's house.


The Dokkaebi was slouched on the sofa,
the TV on.

The Messenger asked,
"What are you doing?"

"What does it look like?"
the Dokkaebi said.
"Got scolded for no reason.
Just watching TV."

Grim smiled.
"You know how he is."

"What did I even do wrong?"
the Dokkaebi grumbled.
"All I said was that I like vegetable hobbang."

"Today wasn't a day to be picky,"
the Messenger said.
"He's been worried about you.
With MCGW—Master Chef in the Ghost World—coming up and all."

The Dokkaebi sat up straight.
"Really?"

Grim nodded.

"He says you cook well,
but he's not sure you understand the judging criteria."

"The judging criteria?"
The Dokkaebi blinked.
"Isn't it enough if the food tastes good?"

The Messenger laughed.

"See?
That's exactly what he meant.
You're supposed to know five criteria."

Then he showed the list to the Dokkaebi.

The Dokkaebi fell silent.

Suddenly, he raised his hand.

"Taste."

He folded his thumb.

"Next is... plating, right?"

He folded his index finger.

"Artistry..."

The middle finger went down.

"Creativity..."

Then the ring finger.

"And... following the rules."

He folded his little finger.

His hand closed into a fist.

He clenched it once,
then slowly opened it.

"They look at all of this?"

His shoulders sank.

"I really didn't know," he said.
"I thought good food was enough."

Grim spoke quietly.

"He takes good care of us.
We just don't always understand what he's thinking."

The Messenger hesitated, then added,

"And... this isn't something we're supposed to say."

The Dokkaebi looked up.

"Your newlywed house—
he arranged it through the King of the Underworld.
It's one of the official residences."

The Dokkaebi froze.

"Everyone knows about it in the underworld,"
the Messenger said.
"You live in the human world,
so you didn't."

The Dokkaebi said nothing for a long time.

"I was really foolish," he muttered.
"I'm ashamed."

Then the Messenger pulled out three bags.

Vegetable hobbang.
Pizza hobbang.
Plain hobbang.

"He told us to share them,"
Grim said.

"For friends,"
the Messenger added.
"Today, the three of us—
he said it would be good if we became friends."

The Dokkaebi stared at them.

"Friends... us?"

After a moment, he stood up.

"Then come in," he said.
"Let's steam the hobbang."

That night,
at the Dokkaebi's house,
they steamed hobbang together
and became friends.

chapters.title: Scene 4 - First Love
chapters.content:
One summer evening,
my mother came home
with her skirt filled with balsam flowers
she had picked along the village road.


She put the blossoms into a small mortar
and began to grind them.
Then she handed my sister a 100-won coin.


"Hey—
go to the pharmacy and buy some alum."


When my sister returned,
laughing with her friends,
Mother mixed it in
and kept grinding.


Then she said,
"Go to the room
and bring me some sewing thread and scissors."


When my cousin brought the scissors,
Mother pressed a few plastic bags into her hand.


"Cut them into little squares,
about two finger joints wide—
both ways."


When Mother said,
"Go wash your hands well,"
we all went, giggling for no reason at all,
and washed our hands.


Mother carefully placed
the crushed balsam onto my older sister's fingernails,
wrapped them with the pieces of plastic,
and tied them with thread.


Twenty or thirty minutes later,
every woman in the house
had plastic-wrapped fingertips,
puffed up like little frogs.

Mother said,


"If the balsam stain stays
until the first snow falls,
your first love will come true."


She also said that
even if it hurt a little at night,
we had to endure it.


The next day,
Mother went out again and picked flowers,
then mixed flour into a simple dough.


"You need a full belly
to feel like living," she said,
pouring oil into a frying pan.


On round pieces of dough,
about ten centimeters across,
she placed flower petals
and made pancakes.


I didn't eat any—
I disliked greasy food—
so Mother said,


"You're just eating the flower's scent,"
and put a bite into my mouth.


Whenever Mother did something,
the women of our village rejoiced
as if it were a feast day.


That night,
I grumbled at my wife, Seonju, and said,


"Hey, little frog—
why did you even bother
dyeing your nails with balsam?"


She said Mother had told her,


"A woman must be beautiful,"


and she smiled,
admiring the deep pink color
on her fingers.

I asked,


"So who was your first love?"


My wife answered,


"The son of the woman
who dyed my nails with balsam."




I said,


"You chose the right person."

chapters.title: Scene 5 - Rice Cake or Bread?
chapters.content:
The Dokkaebi entered the MCGW,

a global cooking competition broadcast live
to both the living and the dead on GBS.

Anchors narrated the scenes with practiced excitement
as ghosts from around the world prepared their dishes.


Anchor 1

"Each contestant has brought rare ingredients
representing their home countries."

Anchor 2
"China has shark fin.
France has red and white wine.
And the United States—well—
has a massive tomahawk steak."

Anchor 1
"But the Korean contestant, the Dokkaebi,
seems to have brought very little."

Anchor 2
"Flour, a bouquet of flowers, and a bottle of alcohol.
Is he in the right competition?"

Cooking began.

The time limit was two hours.

Ten minutes in

While other contestants chopped, seared, and flambéed,
the Dokkaebi mixed flour and water into a simple dough,
then sat down.

He stared into space.

One hour in

He stood up briefly,
boiled water,
