placed the dough into a steamer,
and sat back down again.

The cameras lingered, uncertain.

One hour and thirty minutes

He turned off the heat
and lifted something from the steamer.

The dough had risen.

Not into a cake,
but into something closer to a loaf.

One hour and forty minutes

He plated.

He decorated the surface with flowers from the bouquet—
not as garnish,
but as if returning them
to where they belonged.

Time's up

The Dokkaebi presented five plates—
three for the judges,
two for the anchors.

When his turn came,
the judges asked their questions.

Judge 1
"Why did you make this dish?"

Dokkaebi
"I wanted to reproduce
the taste of nature, as it is."

Judge 2
"This is chewy, softly sweet.
Did you use sugar?"

Dokkaebi
"No.
I used acacia honey.
During fermentation,
the yeast consumes the sugar
and creates air pockets inside the dough.
That's where the softness comes from."

Judge 3
"But you didn't add any commercial yeast."

Dokkaebi
"I mixed water and makgeolli
in a seven-to-three ratio.

Makgeolli—sparkling rice wine with live cultures—
is a living fermented rice wine.
It already contains yeast."

Judge 1
"So fermentation did the cooking."

Dokkaebi
"Yes.

Cooking, to me,
is simply helping yeast
reach its best moment."

Judge 2
"And this aroma—
where does it come from?"

Dokkaebi
"The floral scent of the acacia honey.

The yeast eats the sugar.
The fragrance stays."

Judge 3
"And this balance—
soft, sweet,
spongy and cloud-like,
but never overwhelming?"

Dokkaebi
"That's what happens
when you wait."

Judge 1
"Do you eat this often?"

Dokkaebi
"On ancestral memorial days.
And at celebrations."

Judge 3
"What do you call this dish?"

Dokkaebi
"At formal ceremonies,
it's called gijitteok—a rice cake.

On ordinary days,
we call it sul-ppang.
Liquor bread."

The judges exchanged glances
and nodded.

After all evaluations were complete,
the announcement was made.

Judge
"The winner of this year's MCGW is—
not a Korean chef..."

A pause.

"...but Korean yeast."

Epilogue

When I was a kid,
food was never something you rushed.

You waited—
for dough,
for steam,
for people.

The yeast always knew
when to rise.

All we had to do
was not interfere.

Since the organizers couldn't award
a trophy to yeast,
they gave the Dokkaebi
the title of MCGW Winner
and a luxury sedan.

chapters.title: Scene 6 - After the Lights Went Out
chapters.content:
A few nights after the MCGF ended,

the Dokkaebi knocked on the office door.


The Messenger and Grim Reaper happened to be there.
They welcomed him warmly.


They congratulated him.

Messenger
"Hey!
Who dares call you a loser?
You drank way too much tonight.
You should go to bed.
We'll take you home."


(The Dokkaebi suddenly grows philosophical.)


Dokkaebi
"Home?
What is home?
Is it a place,
or a temperature?


Listen—
I'm not drunk.
I'm fermented.
Drunk people fall down.
Fermented people rise.


Also—
why does everyone get credit after it works?
Before that, I was just 'that guy with flour.'
After that, suddenly—genius.


Write this down.
History hates witnesses."


Dokkaebi
"Wait!
Boss! No—General!


Didn't I mix it?
Didn't I wait?
Didn't I steam it?
Did the rice cake walk onto the plate by itself?


People say the yeast did everything.
So what did I do?"


Me
"You did everything.
You took sacks of flour from my house,
bottles of makgeolli, even honey.
You figured out the judging criteria on your own.
You practiced secretly at my place.
All without permission.


That's theft.
That's trespassing.
Your place is a GIA cell, you little punk."


Grim & Messenger
"Boss, please calm down!
The Dokkaebi seems a bit hurt inside!
We'll take him and put him to bed!"


Dokkaebi
"Yes! I'm a thief!
A fool who doesn't even know the rules!
Take me to jail!
No—
send me to the King of Hell's fire pit!!!"


Grim (covering the Dokkaebi's mouth)
"This is getting serious.
Messenger, let's take him out—now."


They dragged the Dokkaebi away.


As he was being pulled down the hallway, the Dokkaebi shouted one last thing:


Dokkaebi
"Hey—!
If yeast did everything,
then at least give it the trophy!
I demand...
equal rights for fermentation!!!"


I spoke quietly.


"That's broadcasting.
And that's the law.
It's not a world that recognizes the truth.
When will he grow up...?"

chapters.title: Scene 7 - Briquettes vs. Steam 1
chapters.content:
The New School Building


When I was in fourth grade, construction began on a new school building. We were still kids, but we cheered anyway— not because we understood architecture, but because it meant we might finally be freed from polishing wooden floors with shellac, rubbing them shiny with the bottoms of old glass bottles.

We wanted to help. At the very least, we thought we should carry a few bricks. It felt only right.


By the time the building was completed, we were in fifth grade. Along with the sixth graders, we moved into the new classrooms. They had steam heating. Double-pane windows. No cold drafts slipping in through the cracks.

The best part was the floor. It was new, coated with wax— all you had to do was sweep it with a broom, and cleaning was done.


Escaping the hell of polishing floors by hand felt like stepping into a different world.


Then, in sixth grade, we were sent back to the old building.


We protested. It felt unfair.


The teachers explained calmly: "If you give way, students from first to fifth grade can study in the new building. And younger kids don't know how to manage or maintain the old classrooms."

Their reasoning was flawless.


Still, we were stunned. Annoyed. Bitter.


We had carried bricks. We had imagined ourselves staying. And now the new classrooms belonged to our juniors.


One afternoon, as the light began to slant and the yard loosened, a baseball game was arranged during PE— fifth graders versus sixth graders. A teacher would be the umpire.


We were determined to teach them a lesson.


I was preparing for a math competition, so I stayed behind, joking, "Hey—don't draw blood. Take it easy on them." I smiled in a way that suggested I meant the opposite.


But twenty or thirty minutes later, my classmates came back to the classroom.


Curious, I asked, "Hey, why are you back already?"


Bang-gu—Cha Seong-hae—clicked his tongue and said, "How are you supposed to play baseball with kids who shut their eyes tight when the ball's thrown at them?"

I laughed and said, "But when we were in fifth grade, didn't we go all out against the older kids? Like it was life or death?"


He shrugged. "If fifth graders these days had that kind of nerve, do you think we'd be stuck like this?"


I had nothing to say. I just let out a hollow laugh.


It felt like both we and that old school building were destined to graduate together.


It wasn't the younger kids I hated. It was the share that had been assigned to us.


And even that share, in the end, turned out to be our fate.

chapters.title: Scene 8 - Briquettes vs. Steam 2
chapters.content:
The Aluminum Lunchbox

By late October, or sometimes November,
we had another ritual to complete.

The school custodian would hand out stove pipes and heaters,
and we had to install them in the classroom ourselves.

The pipe had to be fitted into the exhaust vent,
then fixed along the ceiling and wall corners.

We hammered nails into place,
wrapped the pipe tightly with wire,
and tied it off to both sides.

The bent L-shaped joint was straightened downward
and finally connected to the briquette stove.

That alone could take an entire day.

Every morning,
the duty students arrived early
to collect briquettes, firewood, and ignition charcoal.

If you were late,
your class received fewer briquettes than the others—
so we took it seriously.

Desperately, even.

First, you lit the ignition charcoal
and placed it at the bottom of the stove.

Then came a few pieces of firewood.

Only after that
could you carefully stack the briquettes—thinly—
so the cold, damp coal
could slowly absorb the heat
and catch fire.

Once it did,
you added briquettes one by one,
adjusting the flame.

There were always one or two kids
who naturally took the lead in that kind of work.

In our class,
that kid was O-han.

Shovel in hand,
he fed the stove relentlessly,
controlling the fire
like it was second nature.

"Anyone who wants to take charge of lunch," he declared,
"has to endure the weight of the shovel."

Warming our cold aluminum lunchboxes
was a job of its own.

You'd set a lunchbox on the flat of the shovel,
then rest it gently on the red-hot stove—
move it slightly,
shift it again,
just a little at a time.

With just a few movements of the hand,
the quality of that day's lunch was decided.

Some lunchboxes came out warm on the outside
but still cool inside.

Others smelled faintly scorched—
rice just beginning to burn.

In short,
our lunches lived or died
by O-han's touch.

Back then,
I wasn't close to him.

I only watched from a distance.

But at some point,
he grabbed my lunchbox and said,

"You gotta eat rice while it's hot."

He slid it into the right spot on the stove.

O-han's shovel
didn't care whose lunch it was.

Some kids laughed
when their rice burned a little,
scraping up the crispy bits
like it was a treat.

Others begged him
to burn theirs on purpose next time.

By the time the day loosened
and the bell thinned,
we waited for the stove fire to die out.

During cleaning time,
we shoveled out the fully cooled briquettes
and threw them away.

We opened the windows
and beat the chalk dust out of the erasers.

That was our winter.

And in that cold season,
there were friends
who worked quietly
to keep each other warm.

chapters.title: Scene 9 - Jangnal (Market Day 1)
chapters.content:
Among the valleys of Eunpunggol,

Ugok-dong was also called the market village.

Back then,
a five-day market opened regularly,
where information, food, farming tools,
and household goods were traded.

Our family mainly dealt in rice.

Around our house,
grain-selling ajummas from the township
would set up their stalls,
carrying large sacks slung over their shoulders
with cloth straps.

People from every valley, stream, and hamlet
brought what they had harvested—
soybeans, buckwheat, millet, sorghum, red beans—
and trading them by doe and mal
was simply part of daily life.

Whenever rice sacks had to be moved,
Mother would call out,

"Hey, Chubby—come help with this."

I wasn't particularly fat,
so I always wondered why that nickname stuck.

In truth,
it was an unspoken signal—
calling someone by a warm, familiar nickname
made more sense than using real names
in a crowded market
where voices overlapped
and identities blurred.

On one side,
fish stalls would open as well,
especially before holidays.

Frozen pollock and mackerel
were traded in large quantities.

Whenever I stopped by Taehee's house—
the mill house—
the distinctive nutty smell of the mill
would tickle my nose.

Sesame seeds were roasted
and poured into the oil press,
and after waiting a while,
oil would stream out of the machine.

A funnel was placed
into an empty soju bottle,
and we waited.

At first, the oil ran clear and transparent,
but as time passed,
it turned dark and murky.

Back then,
there were no proper caps,
so plastic bags were folded several times,
placed over the bottle mouth,
and tied with a yellow rubber band—
that was enough.

Watching rice cakes being pulled out
was fascinating too.

If I stood nearby,
the ajumma would snip off a piece with scissors
and hand it to me.

It must have been at least thirty centimeters long.

At first it was pure white,
but as I carried it around and ate it,
it quickly turned black
with hand grime and market dust.

Seeing this, Mother would say,

"You've got a weak body—
how can you eat food covered in dust and snot?"

She'd snatch the rice cake away
and toss it into the bowls
of the dog and the cat.

Most unusual of all,
stir-fried grasshoppers were also traded.

Whenever I passed by,
someone would press a few into my hand.

Black, shaped like tiny twigs,
slick yet crunchy—
when you bit into them,
they were nutty and salty.

Sometimes there were sacks of silkworm cocoons.

Knowing they were the raw material for silk
felt miraculous.

I'd get two cocoons,
touch them,
tear them apart,
and wonder how on earth
this could turn into thread.

And from time to time,
when Donari ajusshi—
who came down from Jeongjachon—appeared,
Mother would greet him,

"Had breakfast yet?"

Back then,
asking if someone had eaten
was the standard greeting.

When I bowed as well,
he'd say,

"You studying hard?"

and walk on.

When I asked Mother
why he was called Donari ajusshi
even though he was part of our extended family
living near our village,
she brushed it off, saying
he was just from a place called Donari.

My friends from Jeongjachon
would joke that Donald Duck grandpa
lived in their village
and laugh about it.

At the center of the village
were the police station,
the township office,
and the agricultural cooperative,
which split the market
into two distinct zones.

Our house was closer to the mountains,
so that side was called the upper village,
and the opposite side
naturally became the lower village.

The atmosphere was completely different there.

The cattle market opened in the lower village,
and there was even a coffee shop.

While the upper village market
focused on everyday necessities and food,
mainly run by women,
the lower village market
was dominated by men—
small traders, livestock dealers, and cattle.

Once in a while,
a cow would go wild.

Its owner would rush in,
grab the reins,
slap the cow's back a few times,
and the animal would quickly calm down.

I found those scenes frightening
and avoided that part of the market
whenever I could.

One day,
cattle traders who had been keeping their money
at our house came to retrieve it.

As they left,
they pulled out a ten-thousand-won bill
from a thick wad
and handed it to me.

After they were gone,
Mother asked me,

"How much is one geun—about 600 grams—of pork?"

"About 1,700 won."

"Then how many geun
can you buy with ten thousand won?"

"About six."

"With six geun,
that man's whole family—thirteen people—
gets a feast.

Did you ever think
that because of you,
they might not get to eat meat?"

"I get it, I get it.
They gave it to me, so I took it!"

I answered stubbornly,
but after that day,
whenever money appeared,
I quietly slipped away.

Sometimes Father would say
we were going to the hyeon,
and I'd follow him—
it was Eunsan.

At school,
I had learned that a hyeon
was an administrative unit
governed by a magistrate
during the Joseon Dynasty,
so I guessed this must once have been
the center of Eunpunggol.

Looking closely,
it resembled the atmosphere
of the Korean Folk Village
I'd seen on TV—
houses and fields aligned parallel along the road,
massive wooden gates
like those of government offices,
and at the village entrance,
in front of a large warehouse,
an open space as big as a schoolyard.

It looked just like our own marketplace.

After the Korean War,
during economic development,
a main road was built through Yecheon-eup,
and commerce likely shifted away from our village.

By around my fifth year of elementary school,
the roads were fully paved with concrete,
and people from Eunpunggol
increasingly went straight into town.

With rural depopulation,
the populations of Eunpung-myeon and Hyoja-myeon
shrank rapidly,
and the traders' bundles in Yecheon
grew smaller.

The diesel engine at the mill fell silent.

As access to town became easier,
Ugok-dong—like Eunsan—
was slowly turning into nothing more
than a quiet rural village.

chapters.title: Scene 10 - Jangnal (Market Day 2)
chapters.content:
One day, following Mother into town, I saw that the market was divided into several distinct sections. When we reached the grain market, the houses of the ajummas who used to sell in front of our home were arranged in a ring around it. We passed by with nothing more than a slight bow of the head.


Mother stopped by the house of President Kim Seong-ryeon. The man greeted us warmly. The building was a Western-style house—what people back then would have called a mixed-use structure. The first floor was the shop; the second floor was where the family lived. On the first floor, the ajumma was busy bargaining and trading. Upstairs, the man was organizing ledgers and lists of telephone numbers for city clients—Daegu, Seoul.



Mother let out a sigh before speaking.


"Business isn't what it used to be, is it?"


The man replied,
"That's how it is here. It's not easy for you either, ajumma."


Mother said,
"We should be looking for another way now, but the man of our house won't hear of it."

The man answered,
"For Dong-gi's sake at least, you should start preparing to move to the city."


Mother nodded.
"We went through the war, and just when it felt like we could finally eat our fill, who knows where the world is headed now."


The man said,
"Your cooking is the best in Yecheon. You've got connections at the county office and all the institutions—if you opened a high-end meat or naengmyeon restaurant, customers would never stop coming."


Mother smiled faintly.
"I've thought many times about just taking Dong-gi and running off to Seoul."


"I understand that feeling,"
the man said.


The two of them parted with a sigh, and Mother and I boarded the bus heading home.


I asked her,
"He looks stronger than the ajumma—why is he the one doing the ledger work?"


Mother replied,
"When orders come in from the city, someone has to load dozens of rice sacks onto a truck and travel to town. That kind of work is too heavy and too dangerous for women."


From the time I entered elementary school, Mother often told me stories about Seong-ryeon ajusshi's experiences in the Korean War.


How he advanced north with the UN forces, scooping icy water from the Amnok River, rejoicing that reunification was at hand.
How the Chinese army surged south endlessly in human-wave attacks, and with no ammunition left, they had no choice but to retreat.
How near the 38th parallel, locked in hand-to-hand combat and with nothing left to eat, he cut flesh from human bodies to feed his subordinates.


I grew up hearing that it was because she had been so deeply influenced by him that she raised her own son—me—with such strict discipline. Naturally, I had no choice but to accept that severity. And somewhere inside, I already sensed that I was destined to leave Eunpunggol.


That day, Eunpunggol, seen through the bus window,
was quiet—
like fields after market day.

Even when the wind passed through,

no one came back.

And I,
was walking back
into that silence.

chapters.title: Scene 11 - Hit-and-Run
chapters.content:
The Dokkaebi had not been seen for weeks.

I was curious about where he had gone,
but considering the passion and effort he had poured into the MCGW,
I decided he needed time to recover from the shock.
I waited for him to come back on his own.

Then one day—

Agent M, the Grim Reaper, the Messenger, and Huldra burst into my office,
all breathing hard.

Agent M
"General! We have a serious problem."

Me
"What now?"

Agent M
"GIA agents showed up and arrested the Dokkaebi!"

Me
"For stealing a little flour? They're making a fuss over that?"

Grim Reaper
"I don't think it's that simple.
This time... it's different."

Me
"What, did he leak classified information while drunk?
What secrets could he possibly know?"

Messenger
"No, sir.
It's... hit-and-run."

Me
"Hit-and-run?
Since when does a Dokkaebi own a car?"

Huldra
"During the last MCGF,
he received a vehicle as a prize instead of yeast...
He drove it, hit another ghost,
and ran away!"

Me
"Oh my Goddddddddddddddddddd—
That's beyond my authority!
Even the King of Hell can't touch this case!
I can't lock him up at home either—!"

At that moment, GIA agents entered the office,
dragging the Dokkaebi with them.

Agent 007
"Sir.
We will briefly report the warrant and the case details
before transferring the suspect."

Me
"You don't normally report to me under GIA procedure, do you?"

Agent 003
"No, sir.
But our Director instructed us
to extend special courtesy to the former Director."

Me
"You all work hard.
I suppose I made things complicated.
You brought the warrant?"

Agent 008
"Yes, sir. Here it is."

(I read the warrant.)

Me
"Unlicensed drunk driving.
Collision with a passing ghost.
Fleeing the scene without rendering aid."

Me
"What's the suspect's statement?"

Agent 008
"He admits to drunk driving.
Claims he was so intoxicated
he didn't realize he hit anyone."

Me
"Is he insane?
Proceed by the book.
And thank the Director for his consideration."

GIA Agents
"Yes, sir."

After they left,
Huldra collapsed into tears.

Messenger
"What will happen to the Dokkaebi now?"

Me
"He'll be locked up in a GIA prison cell.
I'd say at least two hundred years."

Grim Reaper
"The underworld or GIA—
both are equally strict.
Isn't there any way to reduce the sentence?"

Me
"If there were,
the Director wouldn't have told them to report to me.
I wrote the regulations myself."

Agent M
"By the way...
what exactly is the Ghost Intelligence Agency?"

Me
"It was founded around 3000 BCE by Gilgamesh.
Back then, gods and ghosts were harassing humans—and each other—
so an intelligence and policing organization became necessary.
King Sejong, the 45th Director, established the legal framework.
Before I became the 46th,
the organization didn't even have a proper name,
so I redesigned the entire structure."

Agent M
"Then why doesn't anyone know about it?"

Me
"Too much classified work.
Humans refer to it as things like
the Freemasons or the Illuminati—
whatever fits within their limits of knowledge."

Agent M
"Ah... that explains it."

Me
"You're thinking exactly what you think."

Then I turned to Huldra.

Me
"I'll give you a choice.
Think carefully.
You can stay in Korea without the Dokkaebi—
or return to Odin's kingdom."

Agent M
"That's too cruel!
How can you say that?"

Me
"It's a minimum of two hundred years.
No visits allowed.
You know better than anyone
what life without a husband feels like.
Everyone, go home for today."

They all left.

I remained alone in the office,
drinking bitter coffee.

The lights stayed on.

chapters.title: Scene 12 - Transfer
chapters.content:
From the fourth grade of elementary school, I began hearing words like FTA from people who visited the county office or came to our house. My parents started making plans to move to another transportation and commercial hub. But every time the deal to sell our family's warehouse reached the point of signing, it fell apart.


Then one day, a buyer offered the original price plus ten percent. Just as the deal was about to close, another offer came in—from a family with long-standing ties to my father—at ten percent below the original price.


My father said,
"Even so, we ought to help a family we have ties with make a living,"
and went ahead with that deal.


I stayed at my maternal uncle's house in Seoul and went to school there, while Mother looked around for a house and a shop location. Since Mother was originally from Seoul and I had spent many school vacations there, adjusting to school wasn't too difficult.


We signed a contract to buy a house in Seoul, and it finally felt like things were settling into place. Then one day, Father called from the countryside. The family we had ties with was now trying to slash the price unreasonably.


Mother was furious.


"We're going back home and setting this right," she said, packing our things.


I had no choice but to follow.


On the bus ride back to our hometown from the Majang-dong terminal, Mother finally broke down and cried.


Even to my young eyes, the road ahead looked bleak. Nothing about the future was predictable. But one thing was clear. I spoke to Mother.


"Mom. When we get back to the countryside, don't say anything about warehouses or deals. Just tell people we came back because I couldn't adapt to life in Seoul."


"Is that really alright?" she asked.


"I'm still a kid. People will just think, 'I guess that happens.' But if they hear you and Dad got cheated, they'll see us as easy targets and come after us. Then we won't be able to do business anymore."


Mother said nothing.


After we returned home, both the warehouse deal and my school transfer were reset to square one. One day, Father and I were left alone at home. He clicked his tongue and said,


"So, you were acting all smart, but couldn't even adapt in Seoul?"


My patience, which I had been holding onto, finally ran out. I let everything inside me spill out.


"Dad, your judgment's gotten cloudy—what do you think you're doing?
Business only works if you believe the other side can pay, and if you believe you can't deceive them. Go ahead—do it your way."


I slammed the door and went to the annex, where my older sister was crying.

"Lend me your jacket," I said.


Without a word, she handed it to me.


That night, I wandered through every alley in the village, thinking about this and that, until morning.

A few days later, one evening when Father wasn't home, my two uncles—Uncle Daeho and Uncle Jongbeom—came over with their wives. Back then, I still wasn't used to calling them small uncles, so I just called them uncles.


Uncle Daeho spoke first.


"I heard everything from your mother. Where's that scamming family? I'll go over there and finish them off."


Uncle Jongbeom, unable to contain his anger, shouted,


"Dong-gi, lead the way. Who are they? A family that bites the hand that fed them—show me the way!"


I didn't answer.


The two of them ranted about killing and ruining people, filling the house with shouting.


I asked quietly,


"Uncles... your kids are growing well, right?"


They answered in unison,


"Is that what matters right now? Your father—"


I said,


"Of course my father's in serious trouble. But your businesses aren't doing as well as they used to, are they?"


There was no answer.


Finally, Uncle Jongbeom said,


"Business has its ups and downs."


"Uncles, cheap rice and raw materials are going to start coming in from the United States. When that happens, the grain trade in the town market and the logging business will shrink—and eventually disappear. If you think about the kids, you should start preparing for something else as soon as possible."


Uncle Daeho scoffed.


"They say that Yankee rice doesn't even taste good. What's there to be afraid of?"


I replied,


"Look at the things those American soldiers sent to our house—the tractor and the Ford Mustang. See how well they're made? This is like throwing eggs at a rock."


The uncles just blinked.


"Uncles, how about running a workers' canteen near the steel mills in Pohang or Gwangyang? It'll be hard to get established at first, but those places won't collapse easily. If you insist on staying near home, then maybe move to Punggi, where Great Aunt's family is, and try dealing in medicinal herbs."


The uncles jumped up in protest.


That's when my second aunt stepped in to calm them down.


"In the last five years, I've never seen Dong-gi be wrong," she said.
"Think about it. My marriage, my husband's life—even mine—we wouldn't be living like this now if it weren't for him."


The uncles fell silent.


I said,


"Uncles, don't think about anything else—just think about feeding your kids. Once things are settled here, I'm planning to go to Seoul too. You don't have to decide right away. Just think it over, slowly."


I left the room.


Everyone walked toward where the cars were parked in front of the warehouse. Then my second aunt suddenly turned back and ran toward me. She grabbed my hand tightly.


"A few years ago, you saved us once already. And now you've saved us again," she said.
"Please, put down that heavy burden you're carrying and find some peace. It's late, but I bow to you for the price of life back then."

She pressed her hands together and bowed deeply, her feet neatly aligned—
a debt of gratitude carried over from her years as a house nanny.


"Sukhee-nuna," I said, lifting her up,
"we'll probably have a hard time seeing each other now. Stop crying. Let's be sure to meet again someday."


A year later, word came that my uncles had opened a medicinal herb shop in Punggi.

chapters.title: Scene 13 - Eorimseong (Royal Overlook Fortress)
chapters.content:
After seeing my uncles off, I went back to my room and sat alone, staring emptily at the janggi board. My wife came in and said,

"I asked Father if you're good at janggi."

"What did he say?"

"He said it's not janggi—you play like you're putting your life on the table. Scarier than a tiger, he said."

"My father-in-law must've gone easy on me."

"No. He said you didn't. He said you deliberately left him a way out. You played as if telling him, kill me or spare me, do whatever you want—and that if he took that move, he'd really lose."

"Did I? Maybe that's so."

"My husband—your heart seems really heavy today. I'll make kimbap. Let's go on a picnic tomorrow."

"Where to?"

"Wherever your feet take us."

The next morning, I told my wife not to dress up and to steel herself. I handed her the work boots and jeans I used at the logging site. She put them on, packed food into a backpack, and we left the house.

After about ten minutes walking toward town, the stream reappeared and a bridge came into view. Following the road that wrapped around the mountainside, we passed Oraesil, where Jeong-hee used to live. Fifteen minutes later, we crossed water again and saw a bridge engraved with the name Geumgok.

"Let's go see a ranch today," I said.

"A ranch? There's nothing but mountains here," she said, tilting her head.

"Just follow me."

After walking the mountain path for twenty or thirty minutes, we passed a small settlement of a little over ten households. Beyond that, we followed a forest trail worn down by footsteps and climbed for about an hour—when my wife slipped.

"Are you hurt?" I asked, helping her back to her feet.

Her palm was scraped and bleeding a little.

"Tsk... clumsy," I said, wrapping her hand with my handkerchief.

"Want to sit for a bit?"

"Yeah. Let's catch our breath."

"Is it that hard?"

"The trail's rough—and why did you make me wear these heavy work boots?"

"Heh... those boots might just save your life."

"What are you talking about?"

"Do you know why these mountain paths are scary? Tigers used to roam here. That's what horan was—tigers coming down to villages and killing people because there was nothing left to eat. These days you might run into wild boar, and since it's fall, snakes are filling themselves with venom before hibernation. If they see anything passing by, they bite first."

Her eyes widened.

"Then what do we do? Snakes scare me the most."

"That's why I had you wear the boots. Snakes go for frogs and mice, but with people they bite the ankle. Thick leather—no pit viper can get through it. From here on, if you slip, you'll roll straight down the mountain. Let's find a branch to use as a walking stick."

I pulled her up by the hand, and we kept climbing. About an hour later, the remains of an old earthen fortress came into view, and beyond it, a wide grassland opened up.

"We're here. What do you think—spectacular, right?"

"Wow... how is there a place like this on top of a mountain?"

"This is called Sky Ranch. Looks like the animals are grazing somewhere else today."

"How do you even know about this place?"

"It'd be stranger if someone from Eunpunggol didn't. They say King Gongmin fled here during the Goryeo period to escape the Red Turbans. Since the king himself came and oversaw the construction, they called it Eorimseong—the Royal Overlook Fortress."

"So what happened to King Gongmin?" she asked.

"You know Eunpunggol's eastern shrine, right? Even during the Korean War, people here didn't know a war had broken out. With ridges and valleys in every direction, and the Taebaek and Sobaek ranges layered like shields, no one could find you even if they tried. People here died of hunger, fell off cliffs while gathering herbs, or met wild boars. Honestly, King Gongmin was probably more afraid of tigers and bears—but he had guards to deal with those."

She sat on the flat ground of the fortress ruins and said, "I get it," taking out the lunchbox and soda.

"What do you want to be, honey?"

"It's not about what I become. I just want to make sure my wife and kids can live without envy."

"Come on... your mother said you're going all the way to America, across the sea."

"I thought so too."

"And now?"

"I learned something during this transfer."

"What?"

"I'm worried about Mother."

"Why?"

"You know I told her to say we came back because I couldn't adapt in Seoul, right?"

"Yeah."

"That's the problem."

"How is that a problem?"

"She shouldn't have done that. No matter what I said. Parents using their child's name for expediency—that's not right. I think even if it hurts her pride and costs her money, she should close up shop here."

"But she's doing well, isn't she?"

"That's the problem. In Seoul, I saw it clearly—you either have specialized skills or serious capital. That's how people survive. Living here for decades, I think she's falling behind the way the world is changing."

"So what are you going to do?"

"I don't think I'll go to middle school. I'll probably take the GED, like my cousin in Jeongjachon."

"Then what about me?"

"I have to provide for you. Even if it costs me everything."

"I can work too!"

"I know. But this country still isn't kind to women. You need a degree just to become a schoolteacher. I'll try harder—no matter what."

"That's too much... why do you carry all that alone?"

I stared at the sky for a long time.

"The sky's really blue today. Guess autumn's getting deeper."

That's probably the fate of men from Eunpunggol, I thought.

Then I laughed and said,

"I was talking nonsense. Sing one of your ABBA songs like last time."

She replied,

"You make me worry for nothing. Let's eat and head back down."

We descended the mountain together.

As we walked, I said,

"Sing ABBA's Dancing Queen for me."

"That's embarrassing... I'll sing it when we get home," she said.

chapters.title: Scene 14 - Separation
chapters.content:
I gathered Huldra—who had chosen to remain in Korea—

and the other ghosts.

Me
"You all know this already.

Humans will leave for the cities.
They will no longer believe in you.

They won't share food with you,
or even speak to you."

Messenger
"Then what should we do?"

Me
"You must find your own lives."

Grim Reaper
"Me too?"

Me
"Everything begins with relationship and trust.

I came to know you.
We talked.
We shared food.

That's how a relationship forms,
and from that, trust is born—
as colleagues, as friends.

There's no exception to this,
whether you're human, a ghost, or in the afterlife.

Humans fear death,
but they will soon treat the Grim Reaper
and even the King of Hell
as nothing more than old stories."

Huldra hesitated.

Huldra
"Then... should I return to Odin's kingdom?"

I shook my head.

I turned to Agent M.

Me
"Agent M.
Will you lead them?"

Agent M
"No!

I'm not eligible for that.
I'm just a woman ghost!"

Me
"Exactly.

A woman ghost.
Competent.
Responsible.
With a strong will."

Agent M
"I'm not ready, sir!"

Me
"Four hundred years ago,
during the Korea–Japan war,
men fought to protect the country,
and women fought alongside them—
caring for the wounded
and protecting children.

You were their leader.
People followed you.

That's why I hired you.

From now on,
you will guide your friends
and the other ghosts
to the place I have prepared."

Agent M
"Yes, sir!
I will follow your order!

But... sir.
Who will remain by your side?"

Me
"I have a family in the real world.
Don't worry about me.

There is a secret door
at the end of the emergency exit.

The key code is my birthday.
You remember it, don't you?"

Agent M
"Yes, sir!"

She turned sharply.

"Everyone, stand up!
Attention!
Bow!"

Every ghost in the room bowed to me.

Me
"Thank you.

It's time to say goodbye."

Agent M began leading her colleagues
toward the emergency exit.

They opened the secret door
and followed a long corridor.

After thirty minutes of walking,
someone was waiting
at the end of the passage.

A very familiar figure.

A male ghost.

The Dokkaebi.

They rushed toward him,
shouting and asking what had happened.

Dokkaebi
"It's a long story.

You know our General prepared
the turtle ship fleet
on the far side of the moon.

He sent me ahead
to prepare your new residence."

Ghosts
"Then what about the hit-and-run?"

Dokkaebi
"They said it was a two-hundred-year sentence
in a GIA prison.

Turns out the prison was this place—
working here for two hundred years.


Guess the boss needed a cover story
to keep things classified."

He scratched his head and laughed.

"Now—

I've cooked ramyeon.

It tastes terrible once it gets cold,
so let's eat first
and talk later."

And so they followed the Dokkaebi
to the restaurant,
where he now worked
as the head chef.

chapters.title: Scene 15 - Good bye Little Groom!
chapters.content:
That morning, I told my wife,
"After lunch, we're supposed to visit your father's house.
So dress up a little, okay?
And you know—official outings need to be reported to my parents first."

After a few hours, we informed my parents about our outing.
Then we began to walk.

My wife was slightly delighted,
but every single step I took
felt as heavy as a hundred miles.

Five hundred meters.
Every corner was still there—
exactly as it had been
when I used to run through these streets as a boy.

When we reached the front gate of her father's house,
right beside the small hospital,
he rushed out the moment he saw us.

I called out,

"Father!
Mother!
It's me!
It's me—your son-in-law!"

My father-in-law burst through the gate, arms wide.

"My son!" he cried.
"You came back to me!
...But who is this girl?"

I answered with a grin,

"Probably a Velcro flower.
She stuck to me on the way here—
and, well... I couldn't shake her off."

My wife shot me a glance—
eyes half-open,
half-annoyed,
and maybe, just maybe,
trying not to smile.

He called out toward the kitchen.

"Honey! Seonju!
Bring some tea and snacks, please.
The men need to talk."

Then he nodded to me,
and the two of us stepped quietly into the small hospital office.

When the door closed behind us,
he turned to me.

"So," he said,
"you have something to tell me."

I took a breath.

"Yes... Father."

He waited—silent, steady.

"You've probably heard the rumors about my family," I said.
"They're not rumors.
They're true."

His eyes tightened,
but he didn't interrupt.

"My family has fallen.
Completely.
And I don't want your daughter standing under something that's already crumbling."

"It's time to give her freedom.
If she has a baby someday, I'd be glad...
but she must not be trapped with me out of duty.
So this is her last chance—
her real chance—
to choose her own life."

He inhaled slowly.

"My uncle in Seoul works at one of the biggest banks," I continued.
"He told me they're looking for people with accounting skills."

I looked toward the hallway,
where Seonju's shadow flickered in the light.

"She learned all that while helping my mother.
She's good at it.
She's competitive.
She can stand on her own feet."

"She can do well, Father.
But she shouldn't have to do it while tied to me.

He looked out through the window
at the pale fields beyond.

"Autumn is gone," he murmured.
"And winter will come again... just like water flowing downhill."

"When I checked your health two years ago,
you were strong enough to make her pregnant.
But you didn't."
He exhaled.
"You showed me what a real man is."

He nodded, almost painfully.
So I spoke—slow, steady.

"Father...
I know you were supposed to go to the big hospital in Seoul.
But you stayed here—
because of me.
And I've always known that."

He lifted his eyes.

"My weak body was never your fault.
It was simply the life I was given—
my destiny, not your mistake."

"So please...

stop blaming yourself."

He said nothing.

The silence was long—heavy.

Then he spoke again, without pause:

"When you beat every man in the village
at the Korean chess game...
When you became an honored student at school...
When you handled every little and big disaster in this town..."

His voice thinned,
but his eyes burned.

"Every time—
It was my glory.
It was my pride."

He breathed in softly.

"You are more than a son-in-law.
You are... simply my son."

At that moment,
a sharp crack of breaking glass howled outside—
like the wind splitting open.

Then she ran in,
fell to her knees in front of me,
and clutched my hands.

"Just let me stay by your side," she whispered.
"I knew this day would come...
but knowing doesn't make it hurt less.
Please—
Let me raise a child who carries your way of living."


"When you watch me, I feel alive."


"When you smile at me, I feel loved."


"How am I supposed to live without you?"

Tears swelled and spilled onto the floor—
each drop sounding like something breaking inside us both.

"You're crying," I said.
"Crying kids cannot join the game."

She trembled a little.

I looked at her—

small, hurting, brave

in the way only the wounded can be.

"Sorry...

I didn't know life was that kind of game."

"Now you must start a new game without me,"

I told her softly.

"Until we meet again."

I kissed her lips for the first time—
a quiet, trembling kiss—
then wiped the tears from her cheeks
with the tips of my fingers,
as if erasing the last line of a story
I was no longer allowed to finish.

And she didn't say a word.
She just let me go.

When I came home,
my mother asked quietly,

"She's gone?"

I nodded.

"After three years," I said,
and walked into my empty room.

The house was too quiet,
as if it already knew she would never return.

The lights were off.

Nothing had changed—
except me.

Goodbye, my wife.
Goodbye to the era when I was still allowed to be a child.
